<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What role did technological advancements play in shaping the milestones of global production?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Technological advancements acted as an *enabler and accelerator* of global production milestones by changing (1) how firms coordinate across distance, (2) what can be modularized and outsourced, and (3) how reliably flows can be controlled.

### 1) Making global coordination feasible (information connectivity)
A key milestone in global production is the shift from locally bounded supply networks to globally coordinated ones. New ICT (internet, smartphones, digital standards) reduced communication and search costs and made it easier to source knowledge and services worldwide—supporting “global sourcing” and blurring industry borders. (Lecture 2, Slide 22)

**How to think about the mechanism:** when information can move instantly and cheaply, firms can split activities across locations and still manage them as one system.

### 2) Enabling modular production and tighter supplier integration (industrial organization)
As production became more modular and partners could be integrated more tightly, firms could rely on synchronized deliveries and flexible material flows—supporting Just-in-Time-style systems with many collaborating partners close to or integrated into the production process. This kind of setup is a milestone because it reduces buffers and makes multi-partner production networks operationally viable. (Lecture 1, Slide 24)

**Why technology matters here:** tighter integration requires fast, reliable information sharing and process transparency across multiple actors.

### 3) Creating end-to-end visibility and control in logistics (execution capability)
Another milestone is moving from “shipping and hoping” to trackable, event-driven logistics. Barcode/RFID scanning at each handover creates standardized event data stored centrally and shared with shippers/receivers, improving ETA visibility and exception handling. This supports global production by making long, complex transport chains more controllable. (Lecture 12, Slide 43)

**Result:** when transportation is digitally traceable, firms can operate with less safety stock and coordinate across continents with higher reliability.

### 4) Supporting cross-border production configurations (global fragmentation)
Technological change also complements procedures that make cross-border processing practical (e.g., temporarily exporting goods for processing and re-importing with duties based on value added abroad). While these are legal/customs mechanisms, technology helps firms manage the complexity and coordination of such dispersed processing steps. (Lecture 7, Slide 23)

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
In what scenarios would an agile production system be more beneficial than mass or lean production?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

An **agile production system** is more beneficial than **mass** or **lean** when the *market uncertainty and variety are high* and you need the production system to prioritize **responsiveness and flexibility** over pure efficiency.

### 1) When demand is volatile or hard to forecast
- If customer demand changes quickly (spikes, drops, unpredictable mix), agile systems help you respond fast rather than optimizing for stable, leveled output (which suits mass/lean better).  
- Agile is suited to **less predictable environments** where you need **effectiveness** (serving the market) rather than only efficiency. (Lecture 13, Slide 33)

### 2) When product variety is high and customization matters
- Agile production fits settings with many variants, options, or frequent configuration changes—where changeovers, engineering changes, and short runs are common.  
- In contrast, mass production assumes standardized products and high repetition; lean works best when variety is limited and processes can be stabilized. (Lecture 13, Slide 33)

### 3) When product life cycles are short (frequent new product introductions)
- If products become obsolete quickly (fashion, consumer electronics, seasonal items), agility helps you ramp up/down and switch designs fast.  
- This aligns with **short life cycles** and the need to compete on **time** rather than primarily on cost. (Lecture 13, Slide 33)

### 4) When the key “order winner” is speed/time-to-delivery
- If customers choose you because you deliver faster (or can meet urgent/uncertain needs), agile production is typically the better fit than mass/lean setups optimized around cost and stable flow. (Lecture 13, Slide 33)

### 5) When you need buffer capacity and flexible resources
- Agile systems often rely on *flexible capacity*, cross-trained labor, modular processes, and quick changeovers—accepting some “slack” to stay responsive.  
- Lean/mass tend to push for high utilization and scale efficiencies, which can reduce responsiveness under uncertainty. (Lecture 13, Slide 33)

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What role does demand forecasting play in determining whether to use a push or pull strategy in global production?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Demand forecasting is central because it determines **how far upstream you can commit capacity and inventory before you see real customer orders**—which is essentially the push vs. pull choice.

### 1) Start from demand uncertainty: can forecasts be trusted?
- If **demand uncertainty is low**, forecasts are relatively accurate and you can plan production and distribution **in advance** (push) with lower risk of excess/obsolete inventory. This is the “push-friendly” side of the push/pull matrix. (Lecture 13, Slide 46)  
- If **demand uncertainty is high**, forecasts become unreliable; committing to finished goods early is risky, so you delay final production/assembly until you have actual orders (pull). (Lecture 13, Slide 46)

### 2) Forecasting defines the “push boundary” (where forecast-driven planning stops)
Many global supply chains are hybrid: they **push** based on forecasts up to a certain point, then **pull** based on actual demand downstream.
- In predictable categories (e.g., stable grocery-type flows), ordering and replenishment can be based on **long-term forecasts** at a distribution point, enabling upstream stages to run as push. (Lecture 13, Slide 41)  
- In other contexts (e.g., automobiles in the illustrated example), a long-term forecast can still drive upstream planning and inventory of finished units—showing how forecasting sets the decision to produce/stock before orders arrive. (Lecture 13, Slide 43)

### 3) In global production, forecasting links directly to planning and sourcing decisions
Because global operations have long lead times (shipping, customs, production scheduling), forecasting is not just a marketing exercise—it drives:
- production and delivery-date decisions (“what/for whom/by when”), and
- procurement and inventory decisions (“what is needed”), and
- scheduling/capacity loading (“when is it needed”). (Lecture 12, Slide 8)  
It also sits upstream of export planning, purchasing, logistics requirements, and production scheduling—so a forecast-heavy setup naturally supports push planning earlier in the chain. (Lecture 2, Slide 45)

### 4) Practical way to decide push vs. pull using forecasting
Ask these two questions:
1) **Forecast accuracy & horizon:** Can you forecast demand with enough accuracy far enough ahead to cover global lead times? If yes → lean push; if no → lean pull. (Lecture 13, Slide 46)  
2) **Where is information best?** If demand signals are most reliable close to the customer, consider pushing generic components upstream and pulling final configuration downstream (postponement), rather than pushing finished goods. (Lecture 13, Slide 46)

# Slide 22 of Lecture 2 contains information about Intensified by new Technologies, especially ICT
and new rules of competition
This development is intensified by new technologies, especially ICT, and by new rules of competition. The internet has created a “global village”, and international standards such as GCI replace purely national initiatives. With smart phones in your hand, and with the dissolution of emotional links to local craftsmen, industries or retailers (for example, buying cars on the web), global sourcing of technology and know-how becomes common, such as programmers from India or call centres in Ireland. Industry borders are dissolving.

What role does technology play in the management of global production networks?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Technology is a key *enabler* of managing global production networks (GPNs) because it increases visibility, coordination capability, and the ability to balance global efficiency with local responsiveness.

### 1) Technology strengthens “global village” coordination and market reach
Modern ICT reduces the friction of distance: firms can coordinate activities across countries more easily and access global sourcing of skills/knowledge (e.g., outsourced services, digital purchasing, shared standards). This supports the very idea of operating and managing production and supply across borders rather than within national “silos.” (Lecture 2, Slide 22)

### 2) Technology helps align external drivers with network performance objectives
In GPNs, firms must respond to external drivers like supply vs. demand dynamics and global vs. local pressures. Technology (data sharing, analytics, real-time monitoring) helps managers sense these drivers and translate them into performance objectives (cost, growth, flexibility/resilience, innovation/learning, etc.) by enabling faster and better-informed decisions. (Lecture 4, Slide 35)

### 3) Technology enables key configuration mechanisms in global production networks
GPN performance comes from *how the network is configured*—and ICT makes these configuration choices workable in practice:  
- **Inter-firm specialization** (make/buy/partner, supplier development): platforms for collaboration, quality data exchange, and supplier integration. (Lecture 4, Slide 35)  
- **Intra-firm specialization** (product/process scope, location logic, plant roles): network planning tools and standardized information flows to coordinate multiple plants. (Lecture 4, Slide 35)  
- **Global–local balancing** (product/production/business processes): technology supports standardization where beneficial and localization where needed (e.g., modular designs, shared process standards with local variants). (Lecture 4, Slide 35)

### 4) Technology supports “flow systems” and modern production approaches
The course links production planning/design to flow thinking and systems like lean/agile and global production networks. Digital tools help manage flow (planning, scheduling, materials coordination) across dispersed operations—making global networks more controllable and responsive. (Lecture 4, Slide 2; Lecture 11, Slide 41)

# Slide 15 of Lecture 11 contains information about e.g. you could do an ABC Analysis
An example of how you could do an ABC analysis starts with the idea and a checklist of steps. The idea is to use “consumption value” as a selection criteria and to begin with the calculation of the total consumption value of each material per period, where the quantity is multiplied by the cost price. Based on this, you then calculate the percentage with respect to the total number of consumed goods and calculate the percentage with respect to the total consumption value of all goods, and you calculate ranks for the materials. Next, you rank material types in descending order with respect to the total consumption value and classify SKU into different groups. After that, you cumulate these percentages with respect to the total number of consumed goods and cumulate the percentage of the total consumption value of all goods. Finally, you perform the classification of material types in A, B and C goods according to the ABC analysis.

# Slide 28 of Lecture 5 contains information about ABC Analysis,Pareto Principle or 80/20 Rule

Idea: ABC analysis separates out the most important items so that more attention can be focused on those items. It is based on the principle that out of the myriad of items an inventory manager needs to handle, there are only a few that account for most of the inventory expenses.

Checklist: Calculation of the total consumption value of each material per period (quantity multiplied by the cost price). Calculate percentage with respect to the total number of consumed goods. Calculate percentage with respect to the total consumption value of all goods. Rank material types in descending order with respect to the total consumption value. Cumulate these percentages with respect to the total number of consumed goods. Cumulate the percentage of the total consumption value of all goods. Classification of material types in A, B and C goods.

# Slide 29 of Lecture 5 contains information about ABC Analysis – Step 1-4

The image, titled "ABC Analysis – Step 1-4," provides a table demonstrating the systematic methodology used to classify inventory items based on their economic value to a company, which is the necessary next step for prioritizing actions in an inventory improvement initiative. The analysis begins by calculating the Consumption Value for each article, which is the product of the Consumption (in units) and the Price of the item. This value represents the total annual monetary usage for that article. The next crucial step is determining the Consumption value (in %), which calculates the percentage share of each article's total consumption value relative to the overall value of all inventory items. Finally, a Rank is assigned to each article based on this percentage, from highest to lowest. This process allows management to apply the ABC classification principle, where the items contributing the highest percentage to the total inventory value (the high-priority A-items) are identified, enabling the company to focus its limited resources on forecasting, controlling, and optimizing the small number of items that have the greatest financial impact, rather than wasting effort on the numerous low-value C-items.

# Slide 31 of Lecture 5 contains information about Lorenz Curve: ABC-Analysis

The image, titled "ABC Analysis – Step 5-7," is the culmination of the ABC analysis process, building directly on the previous steps of calculating consumption value and ranking items to establish the final classification . This stage involves calculating and evaluating the cumulated percentage of both the item count (Consumption in % cumulated) and, most critically, the Value consumption in % cumulated. By ranking the articles from highest to lowest value (as established in the prior image's ranking step), the cumulative value column clearly reveals the concentration of wealth in the inventory. This data is then used to formally assign the Class (A, B, or C) to each group of items based on the Pareto Principle. For instance, the image highlights that a small percentage of items (A-items) are responsible for a large percentage of the total consumption value, justifying the management principle where the high-value A-items receive the most intensive inventory control and forecasting effort, while the numerous, low-value C-items are managed with simpler, less resource-intensive strategies.

# Slide 21 of Lecture 14 contains information about There are also other criteria? What are the criteria?

This slide explains that, beyond simple cost-based decisions, companies use different analytical criteria to classify materials for inventory control. Two widely used methods are presented: **ABC analysis** and **XYZ analysis**, each focusing on a different dimension of inventory management—purchasing volume and demand continuity.
On the left, the slide introduces **ABC Analysis**, which categorizes items into three groups (A, B, and C) based on their **purchasing volume or value contribution**. A small text box explains that this method ranks items according to their importance:  
- **A-items** represent a small share of total quantity but a very high share of total value;  
- **B-items** fall in the middle range;  
- **C-items** represent the majority of quantity but only a small portion of value.  

Below this explanation, a diagram visualizes the ABC model. The horizontal axis shows cumulative quantity, while the vertical axis shows cumulative value. The shaded regions labeled A, B, and C illustrate how the categories are divided: A-items occupy the steep initial segment, B-items the middle section, and C-items the flatter, long-tail portion.

On the right, the slide introduces **XYZ Analysis**, which classifies materials based on **demand continuity and forecast accuracy** rather than value. A text box explains that this method evaluates consumption patterns to determine how predictable demand is. The classification includes three groups:  
- **X-class:** Items with stable, regular demand and high forecast accuracy;  
- **Y-class:** Items with trend-driven or seasonal demand, offering medium forecast accuracy;  
- **Z-class:** Items with irregular, erratic consumption where forecast accuracy is very low.  

Together, the ABC and XYZ analyses provide a more sophisticated view of inventory management by evaluating materials both in terms of **economic importance** and **predictability of demand**, enabling better prioritization, planning, and control decisions.

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What criteria are typically used to categorize items in the ABC classification system?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

In an **ABC classification**, the typical criterion is the item’s **economic importance**, measured as **purchasing/consumption value** (i.e., how much money the item “consumes” over a period). (Lecture 5, Slide 28)

Step-by-step, what you usually use is:

1. **Consumption value per item (per period)**  
   Compute **quantity consumed × unit cost/price** for each SKU/material. This is the core selection criterion. (Lecture 11, Slide 15; Lecture 5, Slide 28)

2. **Relative share of total value (percent of total consumption value)**  
   Calculate each item’s **% contribution** to the total consumption value across all items, then rank items from highest to lowest. (Lecture 11, Slide 15; Lecture 5, Slide 29)

3. **Cumulative value share (Pareto logic) to set A/B/C cut-offs**  
   Use the **cumulative % of total value** (and often also track cumulative % of items) to assign classes:  
   - **A-items:** few items, high share of value  
   - **B-items:** medium  
   - **C-items:** many items, low share of value (Lecture 14, Slide 21; Lecture 5, Slide 31)

# Slide 15 of Lecture 5 contains information about The Economic Order Quantity

(EOQ) Model
The Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) model provides a way to determine the optimal order quantity by balancing different types of inventory costs. Inventory costs can be classified into purchase costs, which are the prices to be paid when buying items, order processing costs, which are the costs of procuring the inventory, and inventory holding costs, which include warehousing and related expenses. In the following notation, \(D\) represents the annual use of a particular item in number of items per annum, while \(S\) is the order-processing cost, expressed in \$/order. The parameter \(p\) denotes the price per item in \$/unit, and \(H\) stands for the holding cost per unit per year in \$/unit/year. The variable \(Q\) is the number of items ordered in one purchase order, measured in units, and \(T\) denotes the time period between purchase orders as a fraction of a year. In addition, \(SS\) is the safety stock in units, \(L\) is the lead time in fraction of a year and \(I\) is the current inventory on hand in units. Finally, TAC designates the total annual cost of the inventory system. 15

# Slide 20 of Lecture 14 contains information about How much to order? What is the „Economic Order Quantity"

This graph illustrates the core idea behind the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) — finding the order size that minimizes total inventory costs. The horizontal axis represents the order quantity (Q), while the vertical axis shows the cost in euros.
The blue curve slopes downward, representing ordering cost, which decreases as order quantity increases because fewer orders need to be placed. The red curve slopes upward, representing holding cost, which increases with larger order quantities because more inventory must be stored. The black dashed curve is the total cost curve, combining ordering and holding costs. It forms a U-shape: costs fall at first as ordering becomes more efficient, then rise as holding becomes too expensive.
The lowest point of the dashed total cost curve indicates the optimal order quantity—the EOQ—where the trade-off between ordering cost and holding cost is perfectly balanced.

# Slide 16 of Lecture 5 contains information about Derivation of EOQ Formula (1/2)

Assumptions: Order processing cost are equivalent to setup cost as the total sum of
labor and material cost to produce a product, Large lots reduce setup costs, but small lots reduce inventory, Purchase costs remain stable throughout the year and no discount on bulk purchases is granted.
Purchase costs = p x D
Average inventory level = SS + Q/2
Annual holding costs = (SS + Q/2) H
Number of orders per year = D/Q
Annual order processing costs = (D/Q) S

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What assumptions does the EOQ model make about demand and lead time?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

In the basic EOQ model, the key assumptions about **demand** and **lead time** are:

1. **Demand is known and constant over time**  
   EOQ treats annual demand \(D\) as a fixed, predictable rate—so inventory is depleted smoothly and there’s no randomness in usage. This is what allows the model to express “number of orders per year” as \(D/Q\) and build costs around that steady flow. (Lecture 5, Slide 15; Lecture 5, Slide 16)

2. **Lead time is known and constant**  
   Lead time \(L\) is treated as a fixed parameter (not uncertain). That means replenishment arrives exactly as expected, so you can time orders reliably. In the notation, lead time is explicitly included as a fixed fraction of a year. (Lecture 5, Slide 15)

If you want, I can also explain how these assumptions relate to why safety stock \(SS\) is sometimes added (and what changes once demand/lead time become uncertain). (Lecture 5, Slide 15; Lecture 5, Slide 16)

# Slide 9 of Lecture 5 contains information about Inventory Management

The purpose of inventory management is the development of relevant inventory strategies and the achievement of high inventory performance. At the same time, it aims at reducing inventory and related costs as much as possible while still maintaining responsiveness, high customer satisfaction and general operational capabilities. In order to reach these goals, several key decisions have to be made. These include determining the size of the inventory and the appropriate time of stock keeping, deciding when to reorder and what exactly triggers the decision, specifying how much to order or reorder and, finally, deciding where to locate how much inventory in the supply chain.

# Slide 5 of Lecture 5 contains information about A rather messy example…

The image, titled "A rather messy example...," vividly illustrates a massive, disorganized pile of metal parts, likely scrap or salvage from vehicles, filling a storage area where a person is standing atop the heap . In the context of inventory management, this scene represents an extreme case of poor control and unsustainable holding costs. The massive, unmanaged accumulation signifies an excessive amount of inventory, much of which appears to be obsolete (e.g., old car components), thereby tying up capital and demonstrating inefficient asset utilization. Furthermore, the sheer volume and complete disarray lead to prohibitively high non-financial holding costs, as valuable storage space is wasted, and any attempt at retrieval of a specific part would require immense manual effort. Crucially, the lack of any visible organization means that inventory visibility is zero, making it impossible for the supply chain to accurately track or count the stock, which is a fundamental failure to mitigate the "Ugly Tradeoff" between having too much stock and having accurate knowledge of what is held.. <<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What role does Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory control play in reducing holding costs?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory control reduces holding costs by designing the supply chain and operations so materials arrive *when they are needed* (and often in smaller lots), which lowers average inventory levels and therefore the costs of carrying stock.

Step-by-step, the mechanism is:

1. **JIT targets low average inventory**
   - Holding cost is largely driven by *how much inventory you keep on average* (capital tied up, storage space, handling, obsolescence). By replenishing closer to the moment of use/sale, JIT reduces the average on-hand inventory and thus holding costs. This aligns with the overall goal of inventory management: reduce inventory and related costs while maintaining responsiveness/service. (Lecture 5, Slide 9)

2. **JIT often implies smaller, more frequent replenishment**
   - In classic inventory thinking, increasing order frequency (smaller \(Q\)) reduces holding cost but tends to increase ordering/setup/transport costs—so you are shifting the balance in the “how much to order” trade-off. JIT leans toward smaller lots to cut holding costs, and then works operationally to keep the “ordering” side manageable. (Lecture 5, Slide 14)

3. **JIT complements lead-time reduction to cut “pipeline” (transit) inventory**
   - A major lever for lowering inventory is reducing lead times, which also reduces transit inventory and the need to hold extra stock “just in case.” JIT typically goes hand-in-hand with lead-time reduction initiatives. (Lecture 5, Slide 36)

4. **JIT supports broader supply-chain inventory trade-offs**
   - The point is not “zero inventory at all costs,” but managing trade-offs between service level, lead time, capacity, and inventory. JIT is one control approach that pushes the system toward lower inventory while requiring strong process reliability and coordination to avoid stockouts. (Lecture 11, Slide 42)

- **RFID** enables wireless, bulk reading without line-of-sight, so inventory can be identified and counted faster and more accurately than manual barcode scans. This increases real-time stock visibility across locations. (Lecture 12, Slide 47)

- RFID reduces manual scanning effort and data-entry errors, which improves accuracy of inventory records and execution in receiving, picking, and cycle counting. (Lecture 12, Slide 47)

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What are the potential risks associated with global sourcing and how can companies mitigate them?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Global sourcing can deliver cost and capability advantages, but it also increases exposure to several supply chain risks. A useful way to answer is to (1) map the main risk categories and (2) choose mitigation actions that you bake into the sourcing strategy and contracts.  

## 1) Potential risks in global sourcing
1. **Longer, more complex inbound flows → higher disruption risk**  
   Global sourcing typically means more handovers, longer lead times, and more uncertainty (e.g., transport delays, port congestion). Complexity itself becomes a risk factor. (Lecture 4, Slide 38; Lecture 6, Slide 5)

2. **Geopolitical, regulatory, and trade risks**  
   Crossing borders introduces exposure to tariffs, sanctions, export controls, customs delays, and sudden policy shifts—risks that are typically lower in local sourcing. (Lecture 6, Slide 5)

3. **Cost risk / “total cost ends up higher than expected”**  
   Even when unit prices are lower, the *total* cost can increase due to logistics, buffers, expediting, quality issues, or coordination effort—similar to the outsourcing risk where total costs can exceed the in-house alternative. (Lecture 6, Slide 19)

4. **Supplier opportunism and performance risk**  
   Distance and information asymmetry can increase the chance of opportunistic behavior (e.g., hidden quality reductions, renegotiations, non-compliance), a classic outsourcing-related risk. (Lecture 6, Slide 19)

5. **Loss of critical know-how / dependency risk**  
   When you rely on external/global suppliers for important components or processes, you may lose internal capabilities and become dependent—also highlighted as an outsourcing risk. (Lecture 6, Slide 19)

## 2) How companies can mitigate these risks (step-by-step)
1. **Build a robust sourcing strategy (not just supplier selection)**  
   Define requirements up front: spend, risk level, whether it’s one-off vs. recurring, market maturity, number of potential suppliers, contract duration, and improvement potential. This ensures risk is explicitly designed into the decision, not treated as an afterthought. (Lecture 6, Slide 3)

2. **Use multi-sourcing / regional diversification for critical items**  
   Avoid single points of failure by splitting volumes across suppliers and/or geographies—especially for high-risk categories. This directly addresses disruption and geopolitical concentration risk. (Lecture 6, Slide 3; Lecture 6, Slide 5)

3. **Combine global and local sourcing (“hybrid” footprint)**  
   For items needing responsiveness or high availability, keep a local/nearshore option; use global sourcing where efficiencies dominate. This reduces lead-time exposure while retaining cost advantages. (Lecture 6, Slide 5)

4. **Strengthen contracts, governance, and incentives**  
   Since opportunism is a key risk, mitigate with clear SLAs/KPIs, quality clauses, audit rights, penalties/bonuses, and structured performance reviews. Align contract duration with the market/technology lifecycle so you’re not locked in too long. (Lecture 6, Slide 19; Lecture 6, Slide 3)

5. **Protect critical know-how**  
   Decide what must remain core vs. what can be sourced. Use measures like process documentation, dual engineering ownership, training, IP provisions, and avoiding outsourcing the “crown jewels” where capability loss would be costly. (Lecture 6, Slide 19)

What role does supplier performance evaluation play in the ongoing procurement process?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Supplier performance evaluation is central to the **“Manage”** stage of the procurement process: it is how you ensure that what was promised in the contract is actually delivered over time—and how you improve future sourcing decisions.

Step-by-step, its role looks like this:

1. **Confirms contract deliverables are met (control + compliance)**  
   In ongoing procurement, you need a way to verify that the supplier meets the agreed requirements (quality, delivery, service, etc.). This is why the procurement process emphasizes managing the contract against clear deliverables. (Lecture 6, Slide 8)

2. **Creates a KPI-based basis for managing suppliers (performance management)**  
   Performance evaluation translates the contract requirements into **success criteria/KPIs** (e.g., on-time delivery, defect rates, responsiveness). These KPIs make supplier discussions fact-based and enable corrective actions when performance slips. (Lecture 6, Slide 8)

3. **Supports better supplier relationships and continuous improvement**  
   Regular evaluation helps identify where performance can improve and provides a structured way to drive improvements (and document outcomes) during the contract period—rather than only reacting when something goes wrong. (Lecture 6, Slide 8)

4. **Feeds “lessons learned” back into future sourcing and selection**  
   Supplier evaluation doesn’t just affect the current contract—it informs the next cycle of procurement by capturing lessons learned and refining specifications, selection criteria, and risk assessments for future tenders. (Lecture 6, Slide 8)

5. **Helps reassess supplier suitability over time (short-term and long-term capability)**  
   Ongoing evaluation checks both **static, short-term performance** (quality, dependability, flexibility, total cost) and **dynamic, long-term value** (innovation potential, willingness to share risk, long-term commitment). That ensures you’re not just buying performance today, but capability for tomorrow. (Lecture 11, Slide 25)

In what ways can effective communication enhance buyer-supplier relationships in outsourced supply chain processes?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Effective communication enhances buyer–supplier relationships in outsourced supply chain processes mainly by improving **alignment, coordination, transparency, and the “right” level of collaboration** for the specific purchase and relationship type.

### 1) Creates shared understanding of scope and expectations (reduces misunderstandings)
- Use communication to clarify *what is being outsourced*, service levels, quality specs, handover points, responsibilities, and escalation paths. This helps prevent role ambiguity that often harms outsourced arrangements. (Lecture 11, Slide 43)

### 2) Improves coordination and integration across organizational boundaries
- Outsourcing increases inter-organizational interfaces; frequent and structured information exchange (plans, constraints, changes) reduces coordination failures and supports smoother end-to-end flows. (Lecture 11, Slide 40)

### 3) Reduces demand distortion and operational variability
- Better communication of demand signals, forecasts, and changes helps avoid amplification effects (e.g., bullwhip-like issues) and stabilizes ordering/production decisions between buyer and supplier. (Lecture 11, Slide 40)

### 4) Builds trust and enables deeper collaboration when strategic importance is high
- For strategically important outsourced items/services, communication is a foundation for moving from arm’s-length interaction toward partnership/strategic alliance behavior (joint problem-solving, sharing risks/benefits). (Lecture 3, Slide 37)

### 5) Enables the *right* supplier relationship design for each category
- Communication supports aligning “how we work together” with the purchase’s strategic importance—e.g., basic transactional communication for vendors vs. richer governance and joint planning for partnerships. (Lecture 3, Slide 37)

### 6) Strengthens supply chain transparency and visibility
- Sharing timely operational data (status, capacity, disruptions) increases visibility and supports proactive management—especially important when activities are performed externally. (Lecture 13, Slide 24)

### 7) Supports performance management and continuous improvement
- Regular reviews, clear KPI reporting, and feedback loops allow both parties to detect root causes, improve processes, and refine the procurement/sourcing setup over time. (Lecture 11, Slide 43)

# Slide 24 of Lecture 6 contains information about A Total Cost Approach to Supplier Selection
Unit total cost (UTC) is defined as the unit purchase price amended by an appropriate monetary factor to reflect other pure “hard costs” of an item that arise when selecting a specific supplier. To calculate UTC, a five-step framework is followed. First, all total-cost factors that are important to the organisation must be identified, ideally by inviting all stakeholders to point out cost elements and other issues of interest to them regarding the source of supply under evaluation. Second, a “price adder” formula is developed to translate each total-cost factor into a monetary unit based on its perceived level of importance. Third, a debit (or credit) for each total-cost factor, appropriate to each supplier’s performance in relation to those factors, is added to the supplier’s quoted price. Fourth, the quoted price and all total-cost factors are added together to obtain the unit total cost. Finally, the business is awarded to the supplier with the lowest unit total cost. Source: Harding (2007), `https://www.supplychainquarterly.com/articles/121-gauging-total-cost-supplier-by-supplier`. 24

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What methodologies can be used to accurately calculate Total Cost of Ownership when evaluating potential suppliers?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

To calculate **Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)** accurately in supplier evaluation, you typically combine a **process-based cost breakdown** (to ensure completeness) with a **monetization framework** (to ensure comparability across suppliers). Here are the main methodologies you can use, step by step.

## 1) TCO “lifecycle mapping” (Pre‑transaction / Transaction / Post‑transaction)
**Method:** Structure the analysis by following the purchasing lifecycle and listing *all* cost components that occur before, during, and after buying. This reduces the risk of overlooking “hidden” costs. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)

**How to apply:**
1. **Pre‑transaction:** Capture costs of searching, qualifying, onboarding, and mutual education/training. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)  
2. **Transaction:** Capture costs beyond the invoice price—ordering/admin work, transport, tariffs, inspection, returns, follow-up corrections. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)  
3. **Post‑transaction:** Capture downstream costs such as line fallout, rejected finished goods, field failures, warranty/repair, maintenance, and reputational/goodwill impacts. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)

**Why it helps accuracy:** It ensures *scope completeness*—a common source of error in TCO work.

---

## 2) Activity-Based Costing (ABC) style TCO using cost elements + cost drivers
**Method:** For each lifecycle activity, identify (a) the **cost elements** and (b) the **cost drivers** that create those costs, then quantify them. This is essentially an activity-based approach applied to purchasing/ownership. (Lecture 6, Slide 15)

**How to apply:**
1. Break the sourcing decision into concrete activities (e.g., install, maintain, repair). (Lecture 6, Slide 15)  
2. For each activity, list **potential cost elements** (e.g., downtime, committee time, installation labor). (Lecture 6, Slide 15)  
3. Assign **drivers** (e.g., labor hours, documents, shutdown time, inventory shortages). (Lecture 6, Slide 15)  
4. Multiply quantities by rates (hours × wage rate, downtime × contribution margin, etc.) to estimate cost per supplier.

**Why it helps accuracy:** It improves traceability—cost estimates are anchored in observable drivers rather than rough percentages.

---

## 3) Unit Total Cost (UTC) / “Price adder” model for supplier comparison
**Method:** Convert relevant non-price cost factors into monetary “adders” (or credits) and compute a comparable **Unit Total Cost** per supplier; then pick the lowest UTC. (Lecture 6, Slide 24)

**How to apply (the 5-step framework):**
1. **Identify** all relevant total-cost factors with stakeholders. (Lecture 6, Slide 24)  
2. Build a **price-adder formula** to translate each factor into money. (Lecture 6, Slide 24)  
3. Apply **debits/credits** to each supplier based on their expected performance. (Lecture 6, Slide 24)  
4. Sum quoted price + adders to get **UTC**. (Lecture 6, Slide 24)  
5. Select the supplier with the lowest **UTC**. (Lecture 6, Slide 24)

**Why it helps accuracy:** It creates a consistent, auditable comparison across suppliers—especially when multiple departments value different things.

---

## 4) “Extended TCO” including qualitative/strategic factors (hybrid scoring → monetized or decision overlay)
**Method:** Combine hard costs with “soft” factors (e.g., CSR alignment, reliability in crises, relationship/cultural fit). You can either monetize them (if defensible) or keep them as an explicit overlay to the UTC result. (Lecture 14, Slide 61)

**How to apply:**
1. Define which strategic/CSR/policy factors matter (e.g., recycling compliance). (Lecture 14, Slide 61)  
2. Decide whether to **monetize** (e.g., expected risk cost) or use a **two-stage decision** (UTC first, then apply strategic filters).  
3. Document the logic so it’s transparent and repeatable.

**Why it helps accuracy:** It prevents “false precision” where a cheap supplier wins despite risk/CSR issues that later generate real costs or constraints.

---

### A practical way to combine them (recommended)
- Use **(1) lifecycle mapping** to define the cost universe. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)  
- Use **(2) cost drivers** to estimate each item with credible assumptions. (Lecture 6, Slide 15)  
- Use **(3) UTC/price adders** to compare suppliers on a single unit metric. (Lecture 6, Slide 24)  
- Apply **(4) strategic/CSR overlay** so the final decision reflects broader ownership implications. (Lecture 14, Slide 61)

# Slide 43 of Lecture 12 contains information about Eg. Chain of Events – Tracking in Transportation
# Description of the Transportation Tracking Flow on the Slide 43 of lecture 12

The slide illustrates how **digital tracking** works across the entire transportation chain using **barcode or RFID scanning** at each event point.  
It shows how each status update is captured, stored in a central system, and then made available to shippers and receivers.

---

## 1. **Pickup → Short Haul → Sending Depot**
The process begins with pickup by a courier.

At **pickup**, a barcode or RFID tag is scanned, creating the first event:
- **Pickup**

The shipment then travels via short-haul truck to the **sending depot**, where additional scans occur:
- **V-NI In** (vehicle inbound)  
- **V-NI Out** (vehicle outbound)

These scans confirm that the parcel entered and left the depot.

---

## 2. **Sending Depot → Long Distance Transport → Hub**
A long-distance truck picks up consolidated shipments.

At various points:
- **Hub-In** → scanned upon arrival at the transshipment hub  
- **Hub-Out** → scanned when leaving the hub  

Every transition is logged.

The hub cross-docking step ensures the shipment is sorted for onward transport.

---

## 3. **Hub → Long Haul → Receiver Depot**
The shipment travels again via long-haul truck to the receiver's depot.

Scans include:
- **E-NI In** (entry at receiver depot)  
- **E-NI Out** (exit from receiver depot)

This ensures the item is accounted for before final delivery preparation.

---

## 4. **Receiver Depot → Short Haul → Final Delivery**
The last-mile process involves another short-haul truck dropping the shipment at the final customer.

A final scan event:
- **Delivery**

confirms the arrival.

---

## 5. **Central Event Database**
At the center of the diagram is a **database system** where all event scans are recorded.  
Each scan triggers a status update that is stored and time-stamped:
- Pickup  
- V-NI In  
- V-NI Out  
- Hub-In  
- Hub-Out  
- E-NI In  
- E-NI Out  
- Delivery  

A checklist visual shows which events have been completed.

---

## 6. **Reporting & Visibility**
Information from the central system is sent to:
- **Shippers** (who want to monitor outbound shipments)  
- **Receivers** (who monitor inbound shipments)

Real-time tracking enables:
- Exception handling  
- ETA visibility  
- Customer notifications  
- Proof of process completion  

---

## 7. **Overall Logic**
The slide demonstrates **end-to-end digital traceability**, where:
- **Every movement** of the shipment  
- **Every change in custody**  
- **Every transition between logistical steps**  

is captured through **barcode/RFID event scanning**.

These event triggers control and update the logistics chain, enabling complete transparency and better coordination.

---

## 8. **Key Message**
**Digitization of events enables full tracking and control across the logistics chain — from pickup to delivery — through standardized information points and automated status updates.**

What role do tariffs and non-tariff barriers play in the management of international sales and goods flows?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Tariffs and non-tariff barriers (NTBs) matter because they directly shape the *cost, speed, risk, and administrative workload* of moving goods across borders—so they become core design constraints in managing international sales and goods flows. This is closely tied to the course themes of trade facilitation, economic integration, and what firms must know for export/import operations. (Lecture 14, Slide 23; Lecture 11, Slide 44)

## 1) Tariffs: the “price effect” on cross-border flows
**What they do:** Tariffs are duties/taxes applied at import (sometimes export), increasing the landed cost of a product and affecting pricing, margins, and demand in the destination market. (Lecture 14, Slide 23; Lecture 11, Slide 44)

**How they affect management decisions (step-by-step):**
1. **Costing & pricing:** You must compute total landed cost (product + freight/insurance + duties/taxes + brokerage/compliance costs) before agreeing sales terms and prices. (Lecture 11, Slide 44)
2. **Sourcing and network design:** High tariffs can push firms to source from alternative countries, change production locations, or use regional distribution hubs to reduce duty exposure. (Lecture 14, Slide 23)
3. **Customs planning:** Firms actively look for lawful ways to reduce duty/tax burden on import—e.g., through the choice of customs procedures and how they structure shipments and documentation. (Lecture 14, Slide 23; Lecture 11, Slide 44)
4. **Contracting implications:** Tariff responsibility is often allocated via trade terms (Incoterms), influencing who pays and who carries the risk of duty changes. (Lecture 14, Slide 23; Lecture 11, Slide 44)

## 2) Non-tariff barriers: the “time/uncertainty/compliance effect”
**What they are:** NTBs include product standards, licensing, quotas, sanitary/phytosanitary rules, labeling requirements, security checks, customs documentation requirements, and other administrative controls that can restrict trade without being a “tax.” They often create delays and variability. (Lecture 14, Slide 23; Lecture 11, Slide 44)

**Operational impacts (step-by-step):**
1. **Lead time and variability:** Extra inspections/approvals add waiting time and make delivery times less predictable—so you may need more safety stock or longer promised lead times. (Lecture 11, Slide 44)
2. **Process and documentation workload:** Export/import operations require correct classification, origin evidence, certificates, and compliant paperwork—errors can stop shipments at the border. (Lecture 14, Slide 23)
3. **Service level and customer experience:** NTB-driven delays can cause stockouts, missed promotions, and poor OTIF performance—so proactive planning and visibility become critical. (Lecture 11, Slide 44)
4. **Legal/contract risk:** Because international sales are governed by specific legal/procedural frameworks, poor handling of compliance responsibilities can trigger disputes, penalties, or failed delivery obligations. (Lecture 14, Slide 23)

## 3) Interaction with economic integration & trade facilitation
A key course idea is that **economic integration levels and trade facilitation measures reduce both tariff and NTB friction** by harmonizing rules and simplifying procedures—making cross-border flows cheaper and more reliable. (Lecture 14, Slide 23; Lecture 11, Slide 44)

## 4) Practical management levers to handle tariff/NTB exposure
To manage tariffs/NTBs, firms typically focus on:
1. **Choosing appropriate trade terms (Incoterms) to allocate duties, customs tasks, and risk** between buyer and seller. (Lecture 14, Slide 23; Lecture 11, Slide 44)
2. **Building strong export/import operational capability** (classification, documentation, customs interaction). (Lecture 14, Slide 23)
3. **Improving visibility and exception handling** so border delays and compliance issues are detected early and managed—digital event tracking supports this operational control across transport steps. (Lecture 12, Slide 43)

# Slide 34 of Lecture 7 contains information about Incoterms®

Trade Terms
Trade terms can be industry‑specific contract terms or regional usages that are interpreted differently from place to place or from country to country. International commercial terms, or Incoterms®, provide a common and widely accepted set of standardised trade terms. First introduced in 1936 by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) in Paris, Incoterms® have been revised several times, with the latest revision being Incoterms® 2020. They deal with the obligations of buyer and seller arising from a sales contract and with the apportionment of the costs and risks associated with the movement of goods. Incoterms® can be divided into four groups: Group E (Ex‑Works), Group F (movement of goods arranged by the buyer), Group C (movement of goods arranged by the seller) and Group D (goods delivered). 34



[Lecture = 7] [Slide = 37]

# Slide 37 of Lecture 7 contains information about Further Main Characteristics

Further main characteristics of Incoterms® include the distinction between one‑point and two‑point clauses. One‑point clauses, in which the transfer of risks and costs occurs at the same place, include EXW, FCA, FAS, FOB, DAP, DPU and DDP. Two‑point clauses, where the place of transfer of risk and the place of transfer of costs differ, include CPT, CIP, CFR and CIF.  
Certain Incoterms® are principally applicable for any mode or modes of transport, such as EXW, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU and DDP. Others—FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF—are intended only for maritime shipping and inland waterways, where goods are delivered on board or alongside a vessel in a port, and they are not recommended for container transports. Incoterms® can be used for international as well as domestic shipments and can accommodate arrangements for carriage with either the seller’s or the buyer’s own means of transport in FCA, DAP, DPU and DDP. They have to be explicitly incorporated into a sales contract, for example by stating “[…] according to Incoterms® 2020”, and the “named place” has to be specified as precisely as possible, for instance by using a postal address or a UN/LOCODE (`http://www.unece.org/cefact/locode/welcome.html/`). 37

# Slide 63 of Lecture 2 contains information about Incoterms – Purpose and Scope
In pricing terms, shipping terms and sales terms, Incoterms define the rights and obligations of the parties to the contract of sale with respect to the delivery of goods sold. They clarify how functions, costs and risks are split between buyer and seller for the delivery of goods, as required by the sales contract.

As you move from group “E” to “D”, the seller's risk and cost on the cargo increase, while the buyer’s risk and cost on the cargo decrease.

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What are the key differences between the various Incoterms® 2020 categories, such as 'CIF' and 'FOB'?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Incoterms® 2020 mainly differ in **(1) who does what (obligations), (2) where risk transfers from seller to buyer, and (3) who pays which transport-related costs** along the flow of goods. They must be **explicitly written into the sales contract and paired with a precise “named place/port”** because that location determines the split point(s). (Lecture 7, Slide 34; Lecture 7, Slide 37; Lecture 2, Slide 63)

## 1) The “big picture” categories (Groups E, F, C, D)
A useful way to distinguish Incoterms is by how much the seller takes on:

1. **Group E (EXW)**: Seller makes goods available at own premises—buyer arranges most of the journey. (Lecture 7, Slide 34)  
2. **Group F (FCA, FAS, FOB)**: **Buyer arranges main carriage**; seller delivers to a point early in the journey. (Lecture 7, Slide 34)  
3. **Group C (CPT, CIP, CFR, CIF)**: **Seller arranges (and pays for) main carriage**, but **risk transfers earlier** than the final destination (so risk and cost transfer can happen at different places). (Lecture 7, Slide 34; Lecture 7, Slide 37)  
4. **Group D (DAP, DPU, DDP)**: Seller delivers to destination (seller carries responsibility far “to the right” in the chain). (Lecture 7, Slide 34)

As you move **from E → D**, the **seller’s cost and risk generally increase**, while the buyer’s decrease. (Lecture 2, Slide 63)

## 2) One-point vs two-point clauses (why “cost” and “risk” can differ)
- **One-point clauses**: risk and cost transfer at the same place (e.g., **FOB**). (Lecture 7, Slide 37)  
- **Two-point clauses**: risk and cost transfer at different places (e.g., **CIF**). (Lecture 7, Slide 37)

This distinction explains many confusions: in several “C-terms,” the seller pays further, but risk already transferred earlier.

## 3) CIF vs FOB (key differences)
Both **FOB** and **CIF** are **for maritime/inland waterway shipping** (not recommended for container transport). (Lecture 7, Slide 37)

### FOB (Free On Board … named port of shipment)
- **Category logic**: Group **F** → buyer arranges/pays main carriage. (Lecture 7, Slide 34)  
- **Risk & cost**: Transfer happens relatively early (a “one-point” term), so after the agreed loading/on-board point, the buyer bears both risk and cost onward. (Lecture 7, Slide 37; Lecture 2, Slide 51)

### CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight … named port of destination)
- **Category logic**: Group **C** → seller arranges/pays main carriage. (Lecture 7, Slide 34)  
- **Cost vs risk**: **Seller pays ocean freight to the destination port and also provides insurance**, but **risk transfers earlier** (it’s a “two-point” term). (Lecture 7, Slide 37; Lecture 2, Slide 51)  
- Practical implication: Even though the seller pays to “get it there,” the buyer may carry risk during the sea leg—hence the insurance element. (Lecture 2, Slide 51)

## 4) A simple way to compare Incoterms in exams/cases
When you see an Incoterm, ask in this order:
1. **Which group is it (E/F/C/D)?** → tells you who arranges main carriage. (Lecture 7, Slide 34)  
2. **Is it one-point or two-point?** → tells you whether cost and risk split at the same place. (Lecture 7, Slide 37)  
3. **What is the named place/port?** → defines the actual handover points in the contract. (Lecture 7, Slide 37)

If you tell me your transport mode (container vs bulk) and the “named port/place” you’re considering, I can help you choose between FOB/CIF (or suggest alternatives like FCA/CIP when containerized). (Lecture 7, Slide 37)

# Slide 31 of Lecture 7 contains information about Goods Flow, Flow of Property Rights and Financial Flow

This chart visualizes the **three parallel flows** involved in international trade transactions:  
**(1) the physical movement of goods**,  
**(2) the transfer of property rights**, and  
**(3) the corresponding financial flows**.  

The diagram uses three types of arrows to distinguish these:
- **Solid line:** Goods Flow  
- **Dashed line:** Flow of Property Rights  
- **Dash-dot line:** Financial Flow
The interaction takes place between four key actors: the **Exporter**, the **Importer**, their respective **banks**, and the **Carrier**.

## Goods Flow (Solid Line)
At the bottom of the diagram, the exporter ships the goods to the importer through a **carrier** (ship or airplane).  
The path is straightforward:  
**Exporter → Carrier → Importer**, representing the physical movement of the product from the seller’s premises to the buyer.

## Flow of Property Rights (Dashed Line)
Property rights are transferred via the **Bill of Lading (B/L)**, a crucial transport document.  
The sequence is:
1. The exporter hands over the goods to the carrier and receives the **B/L against consignment**.  
2. The exporter then sends the B/L to the **Bank of Exporter**.  
3. The B/L moves from the exporter’s bank to the **Bank of Importer**—either under **documentary collection** or via a **Letter of Credit (L/C)**.  
4. The importer receives the goods **against presentation of the B/L**.
This dashed-line flow shows that ownership of the goods does not transfer simply by shipping; it is formally transferred when the importer presents the B/L.

## Financial Flow (Dash-Dot Line)
The payment cycle follows a financial pathway between the importer, the importer’s bank, the exporter’s bank, and eventually the exporter.
- The **Importer** initiates payment through their bank or issues a **Letter of Credit (L/C)**.
- The **Bank of Importer** sends the L/C or clean payment to the **Bank of Exporter**.
- Once the exporter has complied with the required documents, the Bank of Exporter **credits or releases the L/C** to the exporter.
This flow ensures that payment is secured before the importer gains access to property rights or the goods themselves.

## How the Elements Work Together
The bottom of the diagram includes a curved dotted line labeled **Sales Contract**, representing the underlying legal agreement between exporter and importer.  
The three flows together show how international trade balances:
- the physical delivery of goods,  
- the legal transfer of ownership, and  
- the assurance of payment.  

The chart highlights the **interdependence** between logistics, documentation, and finance in global trade, illustrating how banks, carriers, and traders coordinate to ensure smooth and secure transactions.

# Slide 33 of Lecture 10 contains information about International Freight Forwarder's Functions

1. Gives advice to customers on the quickest and most economical means of transportation (consultancy function),
2. Gives advice to customers on packing problems (packaging function),
3. Cares for customs clearance (clearance function),
4. Secures compliance with foreign trade regulations and Letter of Credit instructions (documentary function),
5. Makes choice of the most suitable carrier and the conclusion of the contract of carriage (affreightment function),
6. Provides groupage service as a particular contribution to economy (consolidation function),
7. Gives insurance coverage during transportation (insurance function),
8. Gives advice to customers on warehousing and distribution (logistics function),
9. Provides carriers’ as well as forwarders’ documents (fiduciary function),
10. Provides supervision of the movements of goods (supervision function).
11. Credits freights, fees, duties payable at once and bills it later on or collects and submits money on behalf of the consignor (quasi-banking function) or
12. Acts as a carrier on own account (transport function)

What role does the commercial invoice play in international sales transactions?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

The **commercial invoice** is the core document that *translates the sales contract into an operable shipment-and-payment record* in an international transaction. You can think of it as the “anchor document” that links **commercial procedures**, **regulatory/customs procedures**, and **financial procedures**.

### 1) Evidence of the sale and what exactly is being sold (commercial side)
- It documents the key commercial terms: seller/buyer, description of goods, quantities, unit prices, total value, currency, and typically the agreed delivery terms.
- This matters because delivery terms (Incoterms) define how **costs, risks, and responsibilities** are split between seller and buyer; the invoice is where those terms are commonly stated to make the contract operational in practice. (Lecture 2, Slide 63)

### 2) Basis for customs clearance and duties/taxes (regulatory side)
- Customs authorities use the invoice value and product information as a starting point to assess **customs value**, determine **duties/taxes**, and check compliance with import/export requirements.
- This connects directly to the “regulatory procedures” needed to clear goods for export/import (customs declarations, cargo declaration, etc.). (Lecture 7, Slide 3)

### 3) Key document to trigger and justify payment (financial side)
- The invoice is typically required to request payment and to support payment processes handled via banks (e.g., under documentary collection or a Letter of Credit document set).
- In the broader transaction, payment flows interact with documents and logistics; the invoice is one of the standard documents that helps the bank-side process release/execute payment once documentary requirements are met. (Lecture 7, Slide 31; Lecture 7, Slide 3)

### 4) Coordination with logistics/documentation actors (operational side)
- Freight forwarders often ensure compliance with foreign trade regulations and Letter of Credit instructions and manage documentation; the commercial invoice is a central input to that work (e.g., correct values/descriptions for customs and bank document checks). (Lecture 10, Slide 33)

# Slide 45 of Lecture 3 contains information about And next: Mixing the channels and the challenges: Omni-Channels

The image, titled "And next: Mixing the channels and the challenges: Omni-Channels," provides a progressive model illustrating the evolution of retail strategy from a basic, limited focus to a fully integrated Omni-Channel experience . It begins with Single-channel (The Legacy), where customers experience only a single type of touch-point and retailers operate with just one channel. This progresses to Multi-channel (The Reality), where customers encounter multiple independent touch-points, but the retailer's knowledge and operations remain siloed across different technical and functional departments. The next stage, Cross-channel (The Aspiration), represents an effort to bridge this gap, where retailers operate multiple channels but strive to provide a single view of the customer, although operations are still in functional silos. Finally, the model culminates in the ideal of Omni-channel (The Nirvana), which represents the new challenge: customers experience a single, unified brand, not a separate channel, and retailers leverage their complete, single view of the customer in coordinated and strategic ways to deliver a seamless experience regardless of the touch-point (physical store, mobile, desktop, social media, email). The move to Omni-channel demands a complete integration of the physical and digital supply chains to fulfill orders and manage inventory across all customer access points.

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What challenges do companies face when implementing omni-channel distribution channels?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Companies typically face **both organizational and supply-chain integration challenges** when moving from multi-/cross-channel setups to true omni-channel. A useful way to think about it is: omni-channel aims to make the customer experience feel like **“one brand, not separate channels,”** which requires deep coordination behind the scenes. (Lecture 3, Slide 45)

## 1) Breaking down silos (organization + processes)
- In multi-channel, channels often operate as separate “units” with their own goals, budgets, KPIs, and even their own planning routines. Moving to omni-channel requires aligning incentives and decision rights so the channels don’t compete internally (e.g., store vs. online). (Lecture 3, Slide 45)
- Many firms struggle because functions (marketing, IT, operations, store ops, e-commerce) remain **siloed**, even if they *aspire* to a single customer view. (Lecture 3, Slide 45)

## 2) Integrating inventory across online and offline
- Omni-channel requires **coherent, integrated inventory visibility and management** across channels (stores, warehouses, online). This is difficult because it changes replenishment logic, safety stock placement, and availability promises. (Lecture 8, Slide 8)
- Firms must decide how to allocate scarce inventory (e.g., reserve for walk-in customers vs. ship-from-store orders), which can create service trade-offs and internal conflict. (Lecture 8, Slide 8)

## 3) Delivering “seamless” fulfillment across touchpoints
- Customers expect to move smoothly between physical store, mobile, desktop, etc. That expectation forces the supply chain to support multiple fulfillment options (home delivery, click-and-collect, returns anywhere), often with tight lead-time expectations. (Lecture 3, Slide 45)
- The challenge is that omni-channel is not only a front-end marketing topic; it requires **integration of physical and digital supply chains** to execute consistently. (Lecture 3, Slide 45)

## 4) Building a single view of the customer (data + systems)
- Achieving omni-channel implies leveraging a **complete, single view of the customer** across touchpoints. This is hard due to fragmented data, legacy IT, privacy constraints, and inconsistent customer identifiers across systems. (Lecture 3, Slide 45)

## 5) Managing service consistency and availability promises
- Omni-channel raises expectations of **consistent service and product availability** regardless of channel; delivering that consistency is challenging when demand is volatile and inventory is dispersed. (Lecture 8, Slide 8)

# Slide 9 of Lecture 5 contains information about Inventory Management

The purpose of inventory management is the development of relevant inventory strategies and the achievement of high inventory performance. At the same time, it aims at reducing inventory and related costs as much as possible while still maintaining responsiveness, high customer satisfaction and general operational capabilities. # Slide 43 of Lecture 12 contains information about Eg. Chain of Events – Tracking in Transportation
# Description of the Transportation Tracking Flow on the Slide 43 of lecture 12

The slide illustrates how **digital tracking** works across the entire transportation chain using **barcode or RFID scanning** at each event point.  
It shows how each status update is captured, stored in a central system, and then made available to shippers and receivers.

---

## 1. **Pickup → Short Haul → Sending Depot**
The process begins with pickup by a courier.

At **pickup**, a barcode or RFID tag is scanned, creating the first event:
- **Pickup**

The shipment then travels via short-haul truck to the **sending depot**, where additional scans occur:
- **V-NI In** (vehicle inbound)  
- **V-NI Out** (vehicle outbound)

These scans confirm that the parcel entered and left the depot.

---

## 2. **Sending Depot → Long Distance Transport → Hub**
A long-distance truck picks up consolidated shipments.

At various points:
- **Hub-In** → scanned upon arrival at the transshipment hub  
- **Hub-Out** → scanned when leaving the hub  

Every transition is logged.

The hub cross-docking step ensures the shipment is sorted for onward transport.

---

## 3. **Hub → Long Haul → Receiver Depot**
The shipment travels again via long-haul truck to the receiver's depot.

Scans include:
- **E-NI In** (entry at receiver depot)  
- **E-NI Out** (exit from receiver depot)

This ensures the item is accounted for before final delivery preparation.

What impact does inventory management have on the efficiency of online versus brick-and-mortar retailing?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Inventory management affects **efficiency** differently in online vs. brick-and-mortar retail because the **service promise**, **demand patterns**, and **distribution/warehouse design** differ. You can structure the comparison like this:

## 1) Efficiency goals are the same, but the constraints differ
Inventory management tries to **minimize inventory and related costs** while maintaining **responsiveness and customer satisfaction**—via decisions on *how much to hold, when to reorder, what triggers reorders, and where inventory is located* in the supply chain. (Lecture 5, Slide 9)  
Those decisions play out differently depending on whether customers pick up in-store or orders are fulfilled through warehouses to the home.

## 2) “Where to locate inventory” drives efficiency differently online vs. stores
- **Brick-and-mortar:** Inventory is often **decentralized** across many stores to ensure immediate availability. This can improve local responsiveness but typically increases total safety stock and ties up working capital (lower inventory turnover / worse cash-to-cash). The “where to locate how much inventory” decision becomes a trade-off between availability and cost. (Lecture 5, Slide 9; Lecture 11, Slide 46)
- **Online retail:** Inventory is often **more centralized** in DCs/fulfillment centers. Centralization can reduce total inventory through pooling effects and improve inventory turnover, but requires efficient warehousing and fulfillment processes to meet lead-time expectations. (Lecture 11, Slide 46; Lecture 14, Slide 25)

## 3) Warehousing and fulfillment operations become a bigger efficiency lever online
Online efficiency is heavily influenced by **warehouse processes** (e.g., order picking, WMS usage, cross-docking/merge-in-transit) because each customer order triggers picking/packing/shipping work. In-store retail still needs replenishment warehousing, but the “unit of work” is often store replenishment rather than many small e-commerce orders. (Lecture 11, Slide 46; Lecture 14, Slide 25)

## 4) Channel integration changes inventory efficiency (multi- vs. omni-channel)
If a retailer runs **multichannel** without integrated inventory, each channel tends to carry “its own” stock, which can create duplication and reduce efficiency. **Omnichannel** aims for *absolute inventory integration* across online and offline, enabling inventory to be used more flexibly (e.g., ship-from-store, click-and-collect), which can increase availability without proportionally increasing total stock—if managed well. (Lecture 8, Slide 8)

## 5) Performance impact: working capital and logistics metrics
To evaluate “efficiency,” connect inventory choices to **inventory turnover** and **cash-to-cash cycle**:  
- Stores may suffer from slow-moving SKUs sitting on shelves.  
- Online may improve turnover via centralization, but can also face returns and fulfillment costs that require tight inventory control. (Lecture 11, Slide 46; Lecture 14, Slide 25)

### A good way to answer in an exam
Frame it as a **trade-off**:
- Brick-and-mortar: efficiency = high shelf availability vs. higher inventory holding across many nodes.  
- Online: efficiency = lower pooled inventory vs. higher warehousing/fulfillment complexity and need for fast execution. (Lecture 5, Slide 9; Lecture 11, Slide 46)

What are the challenges faced by companies when transitioning from product-centric models to servitised models?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Companies shifting from a **product-centric** model (value delivered mainly through making and shipping a physical good) to a **servitised** model (value delivered through ongoing services around/with the product) typically face challenges in four connected areas:

1) **Operations: managing “inseparability” and customer involvement**
- In services, the customer is often **directly involved in production and consumption at the same time**, which makes delivery harder to “buffer” with inventory and requires tight coordination at the moment of use. (Lecture 8, Slide 23)  
- This creates challenges like: needing more front-line capability, handling variability in how customers use the service, and ensuring consistent service outcomes even when the customer co-produces part of the experience. (Lecture 8, Slide 22–23)

2) **Standardisation vs. variety (process design challenge)**
- Manufacturing supply chains tend to rely on **standardised, repeatable processes**, while service supply chains often struggle to standardise because customers demand **more variety or bespoke solutions**. (Lecture 8, Slide 22)  
- So companies must redesign processes to balance efficiency with flexibility—often by defining which parts can be standardised (modules, service tiers) and which parts remain custom.

3) **Capacity and “perishability” of service**
- Services are typically **perishable** (unused capacity/time cannot be stored), unlike products that can be inventoried. (Lecture 8, Slide 22)  
- This makes capacity planning difficult: firms need to match workforce/asset availability to fluctuating demand (e.g., field technicians, spare parts positioning, remote support availability), and manage peaks without destroying service quality.

4) **Performance management and supply chain coordination**
- Services are **less tangible and more heterogeneous**, which makes it harder to specify, measure, and control quality compared to product specs. (Lecture 8, Slide 22)  
- As a result, companies need new KPIs (uptime, response time, first-time fix, customer outcome measures) and stronger coordination across partners because the “value moment” is often at the customer interface rather than at shipment.

What role does technology play in optimizing reverse logistics processes?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Technology optimizes reverse logistics mainly by increasing **visibility, decision quality, and coordination** across the return flow—so firms can recover more value (reuse/remanufacture/recycle) at lower cost and with better compliance.

### 1) Create end-to-end visibility of returned items
- **Tracking/identification technologies** (e.g., barcodes/RFID/serial IDs, connected product IDs) make it easier to know *what* is coming back, *where* it is, and *in what condition*. This supports the reverse flow from “point of consumption” back toward origin and recovery options (Lecture 8, Slide 25).

### 2) Improve sorting and disposition decisions (“test” and recovery routing)
- Reverse logistics requires deciding whether an item should be **reused, remanufactured, recycled, or disposed**. Technology supports faster and more accurate “test” and routing decisions (Lecture 8, Slide 25).
- **Analytics/decision support** can recommend the best disposition based on predicted condition, processing capacity, regulatory constraints, and expected recovery value (i.e., value recapture is a core purpose of reverse logistics) (Lecture 8, Slide 25).

### 3) Enable cyber-physical systems (CPS) and IoT for condition monitoring and service-based returns
- With **CPS/IoT**, products can generate data during use (health/usage/error codes), which improves:
  - **predictive maintenance** and fewer unnecessary returns,
  - better planning for end-of-life take-back and recovery,
  - more accurate assessment before the item arrives (triage) (Lecture 12, Slide 62).
- This also supports a shift toward selling “solutions/services” (servitization), where take-back and lifecycle services become part of the offering—making reverse logistics more planned rather than reactive (Lecture 8, Slide 28; Lecture 12, Slide 62).

### 4) Optimize collection, transport, and network coordination
- Reverse logistics includes **planning and controlling** efficient flows; technology helps optimize collection routes, consolidate returns, and coordinate actors (collection → test → redistribution/manufacturing) to reduce cost and lead time (Lecture 8, Slide 25).
- Platform/IT integration is especially valuable when multiple partners are involved (e.g., third-party collectors, refurbishers, recyclers), which is common in reverse systems (Lecture 8, Slide 27).

### 5) Support compliance and sustainability reporting
- Because reverse logistics is often driven by **policy/legislation and environmental considerations**, technology helps document take-back volumes, recycling rates, and proper disposal—reducing compliance risk and enabling reporting (Lecture 8, Slide 28).

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What are the different types of warehouse layouts, and what are their advantages and disadvantages?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Warehouse layout types describe how **goods receipt, storage/picking, order assembly, and shipping** are arranged and how material flows through the building. The course highlights three “typical warehouse layouts” based on flow shape: **straight (I-flow), U-flow, and L-flow**. (Lecture 9, Slide 14)

## 1) Straight flow (I-flow)
**What it is (how it flows)**
- Goods enter at one end (goods receipt), move through storage/picking areas, and exit at the opposite end (shipping). (Lecture 9, Slide 14)

**Typical advantages**
- Very clear, linear flow—easy to understand and manage.
- Separation of inbound and outbound areas can reduce interference between receiving and shipping activities. (Lecture 9, Slide 14)

**Typical disadvantages**
- Longer travel distances if storage/pick faces sit between far-apart receiving and shipping ends (can raise handling time/cost).
- Less flexibility if you later want inbound and outbound to share staff/equipment because they are physically far apart. (Lecture 9, Slide 14)

## 2) U-flow layout (often with conveyors)
**What it is**
- Goods receipt and shipping are positioned on the same side; flow goes “down and back” in a U-shape through locations/picking and order assembly. (Lecture 9, Slide 14)

**Typical advantages**
- Inbound and outbound proximity can make it easier to share labor and equipment across receiving/shipping peaks.
- Often supports tight coordination between receiving, replenishment, and dispatch (useful when volume fluctuates). (Lecture 9, Slide 14)

**Typical disadvantages**
- Inbound and outbound traffic can congest the same dock/yard area if not planned well.
- Flow paths can be more complex to control than straight-through, especially with high variety and many simultaneous picks. (Lecture 9, Slide 14)

## 3) L-flow layout (often with conveyor return)
**What it is**
- Receiving and shipping are arranged at right angles, creating an L-shaped flow through storage/picking, sometimes with a conveyor loop/return. (Lecture 9, Slide 14)

**Typical advantages**
- Can fit buildings/sites where a straight line is impossible (space constraints, road access, plot shape).
- Can separate certain activity zones better than a U-flow while still avoiding the “end-to-end” distance of a long straight flow in some buildings. (Lecture 9, Slide 14)

**Typical disadvantages**
- The “corner” can become a bottleneck if many flows converge there.
- Additional handling/control may be needed to manage the directional change and avoid cross-traffic. (Lecture 9, Slide 14)
