<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
How does the integration of technology impact the effectiveness of push-pull strategies in global production?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Technology integration mainly improves push–pull strategies by (1) reducing information delays and uncertainty, (2) enabling tighter coordination across global networks, and (3) supporting different production/flow designs (lean, agile, or hybrids). Here’s how to reason it through:

## 1) Start from what decides “push vs pull”
Whether you should lean more **push** (forecast-driven) or **pull** (demand-driven) depends on **demand uncertainty** and **economies of scale**. High uncertainty favors pull; high scale favors push; some contexts call for a hybrid push–pull (“push-pull supply chain”). (Lecture 13, Slide 46)

## 2) Technology reduces the penalty of uncertainty (strengthens the “pull” side)
ICT and digital connectivity create faster, richer market signals and coordination—shrinking the time between real demand and supply response, which makes pull-based decisions more effective under uncertainty. This is part of the broader “flattening” and global integration enabled by internet/software/mobile tools. (Lecture 2, Slide 15; Lecture 2, Slide 22)

**Implication:** When demand is volatile (e.g., customized products), better information and faster communication make pull more feasible and less costly (you can delay commitment and respond later with better data). (Lecture 13, Slide 46)

## 3) Technology increases visibility and control across the chain (improves the “push–pull interface”)
A push–pull strategy typically needs a well-managed **decoupling point**: upstream might run on push (efficiency/scale), downstream on pull (responsiveness). End-to-end tracking (barcode/RFID events, shared status databases) gives real-time visibility on where inventory and shipments are, enabling tighter replenishment, quicker exception handling, and more reliable execution. (Lecture 12, Slide 43)

**Implication:** Visibility makes it easier to operate hybrids—because the handoff between forecast-driven upstream and order-driven downstream becomes more reliable and less “buffer-heavy.”

## 4) Technology enables global production network configuration (supports both efficiency and responsiveness)
Global production is increasingly distributed (sourcing know-how and operations globally), and industry boundaries blur—this raises coordination complexity. ICT helps orchestrate dispersed partners and capacities, supporting both:
- **Push efficiency** (standardized planning, leveraging scale)
- **Pull responsiveness** (rapid reconfiguration, later customization, faster allocation decisions)  
(Lecture 2, Slide 22)

This connects to the course’s focus on **flow systems** and choosing production system designs (lean, agile, leagile) to match the environment. (Lecture 11, Slide 41)

## 5) Practical takeaway: what “effectiveness” looks like
Technology makes push–pull strategies more effective when it helps you:
- **Lower forecast error impact** via better demand sensing and shorter information lead times (supporting pull where uncertainty is high). (Lecture 13, Slide 46; Lecture 2, Slide 15)
- **Exploit economies of scale upstream** while still reacting downstream (classic push–pull). (Lecture 13, Slide 46)
- **Improve execution reliability** (tracking/traceability reduces disruptions and improves service). (Lecture 12, Slide 43)

# Slide 31 of Lecture 10 contains information about Intermediaries and Service Providers

This slide presents a comprehensive taxonomy of intermediaries and service providers in international trade and logistics, organizing them into three main categories across the top: Intermediaries or Middlemen on the left, Hybrid Forms in the center, and Service Providers on the right. The framework illustrates how different types of organizations occupy distinct positions along a spectrum from pure intermediation to pure service provision, with some entities operating in hybrid capacities that combine elements of both roles.
Starting with the leftmost column of pure intermediaries, the diagram identifies four distinct types. Commercial Intermediaries, labeled CI, include sales agents and brokers operating on commodity markets. These entities facilitate transactions between buyers and sellers without taking ownership of goods or providing physical services, earning commissions or fees for connecting trading parties and negotiating terms. Financial Intermediaries, labeled FI, encompass confirming houses, brokers, traders, and sales agents who facilitate payment flows, provide trade finance, and sometimes guarantee payment to exporters. These entities manage financial risk and liquidity without necessarily handling physical goods. Transport Intermediaries, labeled TI, include customs house brokers who manage customs clearance documentation, cargo sales agents who book space on behalf of shippers, and non-vessel operating common carriers or NVOCCs who issue their own bills of lading while contracting with actual vessel operators. Logistics Intermediaries, labeled LI, comprise fourth-party logistics providers or 4PLs and system integrators who design and manage supply chain solutions without owning transportation assets or warehouses, instead orchestrating networks of service providers on behalf of clients.
The center column presents Hybrid Forms that blend intermediary and service provider characteristics. Export merchants, commission houses, and trading companies operate in a commercial capacity, sometimes taking title to goods, arranging logistics, and providing value-added services while also acting as intermediaries in trade transactions. Commercial banks and insurance companies provide essential financial infrastructure for international trade, offering letters of credit, trade finance, foreign exchange services, and cargo insurance that facilitate transactions while also managing risk and liquidity. The box at the bottom, circled in red to emphasize its central importance, identifies international freight forwarders and cargo consolidators as a critical hybrid category. These entities arrange transportation without operating vessels or aircraft, consolidate smaller shipments to achieve economies of scale, prepare documentation, coordinate customs clearance, and orchestrate the entire logistics chain while acting as intermediaries between shippers and carriers.
The rightmost column identifies pure Service Providers who own assets and perform physical operations. Commercial Service Providers, labeled CP, include entities that provide warehousing, customizing, and repackaging services, performing value-added activities on goods while they are in transit or storage. Financial Service Providers, labeled FP, encompass SWIFT which provides the secure messaging infrastructure for international financial transactions, along with actors operating in financial and insurance markets who underwrite risks and facilitate payments. Transport Service Providers, labeled TP, are the asset-based carriers including trucking companies that move containers and cargo over land, ocean carriers operating vessels on scheduled liner services, and airlines that provide air cargo capacity. Logistics Service Providers, labeled LP, include third-party logistics providers or 3PLs who own and operate warehouses, public warehouses available for general use, and export packaging firms that prepare goods for international shipment.
The connecting arrows throughout the diagram illustrate the relationships and interactions between these different categories. Solid arrows connect the hybrid forms in the center to both the pure intermediaries on the left and pure service providers on the right, showing how hybrid entities maintain relationships with both categories. Dotted arrows specifically connect financial intermediaries and transport intermediaries to the international freight forwarders box, emphasizing how freight forwarders coordinate with financial and transport specialists. The diagram also shows that logistics intermediaries connect to the freight forwarder hybrid box, which in turn connects to logistics service providers, illustrating the flow from strategic supply chain design through operational freight management to physical execution. Transport service providers have an upward arrow connecting to logistics service providers, recognizing that transportation is a component of broader logistics services.

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
In what ways do cultural differences affect communication and collaboration within global production networks?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Cultural differences can shape **how information is shared, interpreted, and acted upon** across firms and sites—so they directly affect both **communication quality** and the ability to **coordinate/integrate** work in global production networks. This matters because global SCM relies on effective **integration and collaboration across intra- and inter-organizational relationships**. (Lecture 3, Slide 3)

## 1) Communication: how messages are sent and interpreted
1. **Direct vs. indirect communication styles**
   - In some cultures, feedback and disagreement are expressed very directly; in others, they are softened to maintain harmony. This can cause misread signals (e.g., “we’ll try” interpreted as commitment vs. polite refusal), leading to planning errors and unmet expectations in the network. (Lecture 3, Slide 3)

2. **Different meanings of “yes,” silence, and escalation**
   - “Yes” may mean “I understand,” not “I agree/commit.” Silence might signal disagreement or respect depending on culture. If partners interpret these cues differently, problems are escalated too late—hurting coordination across the network. (Lecture 3, Slide 3)

3. **Language and translation effects**
   - Even when everyone uses English, varying proficiency changes precision in specifications, quality issues, engineering change requests, and incident reports—raising the risk of rework and delays. (Lecture 3, Slide 3)

## 2) Collaboration: how partners coordinate and build relationships
4. **Trust-building differs across cultures**
   - Some contexts emphasize contracts and formal roles; others emphasize relationship-building and repeated interactions. If one side pushes for quick transactional execution while the other expects relationship investment first, collaboration initiatives can stall. (Lecture 3, Slide 3)

5. **Decision-making and hierarchy**
   - In more hierarchical cultures, decisions may require senior approval, slowing cross-site problem-solving. In more egalitarian cultures, teams may expect fast, decentralized decisions—creating frustration if the partner cannot respond quickly. (Lecture 3, Slide 3)

6. **Time orientation and planning horizons**
   - Different attitudes toward punctuality, buffers, and long-term vs short-term orientation influence how partners handle schedules, forecasts, and responsiveness to disruptions—affecting overall network coordination. (Lecture 3, Slide 3)

## 3) Operational consequences in global production networks
7. **Mismatch in process discipline and standardization**
   - Collaboration often requires shared routines (common KPIs, meeting cadences, change-control). Cultural preferences for flexibility vs strict adherence can create friction when trying to integrate processes across sites. (Lecture 3, Slide 3)

8. **Conflict handling and joint problem-solving**
   - Cultures vary in comfort with open conflict. Avoiding direct confrontation can keep relationships smooth short-term, but can also delay root-cause discussions (quality, delivery failures), weakening continuous improvement across the network. (Lecture 3, Slide 3)

## 4) Practical ways to mitigate (what to do in group projects / firms)
9. **Make “implicit” expectations explicit**
   - Define what counts as agreement, deadlines, escalation triggers, and decision rights in writing (e.g., RACI, meeting minutes with named owners). This supports better inter-organizational coordination. (Lecture 3, Slide 3)

10. **Use structured collaboration mechanisms**
   - Standard agendas, shared dashboards, and clear interfaces between sites reduce reliance on cultural “reading between the lines,” strengthening integration. (Lecture 3, Slide 3)

# Slide 21 of Lecture 14 contains information about There are also other criteria? What are the criteria?

This slide explains that, beyond simple cost-based decisions, companies use different analytical criteria to classify materials for inventory control. Two widely used methods are presented: **ABC analysis** and **XYZ analysis**, each focusing on a different dimension of inventory management—purchasing volume and demand continuity.
On the left, the slide introduces **ABC Analysis**, which categorizes items into three groups (A, B, and C) based on their **purchasing volume or value contribution**. A small text box explains that this method ranks items according to their importance:  
- **A-items** represent a small share of total quantity but a very high share of total value;  
- **B-items** fall in the middle range;  
- **C-items** represent the majority of quantity but only a small portion of value.  

Below this explanation, a diagram visualizes the ABC model. The horizontal axis shows cumulative quantity, while the vertical axis shows cumulative value. The shaded regions labeled A, B, and C illustrate how the categories are divided: A-items occupy the steep initial segment, B-items the middle section, and C-items the flatter, long-tail portion.

On the right, the slide introduces **XYZ Analysis**, which classifies materials based on **demand continuity and forecast accuracy** rather than value. A text box explains that this method evaluates consumption patterns to determine how predictable demand is. The classification includes three groups:  
- **X-class:** Items with stable, regular demand and high forecast accuracy;  
- **Y-class:** Items with trend-driven or seasonal demand, offering medium forecast accuracy;  
- **Z-class:** Items with irregular, erratic consumption where forecast accuracy is very low.  

Together, the ABC and XYZ analyses provide a more sophisticated view of inventory management by evaluating materials both in terms of **economic importance** and **predictability of demand**, enabling better prioritization, planning, and control decisions.

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What are the potential challenges of using ABC/XYZ classification in inventory management?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Potential challenges with ABC/XYZ classification usually come from **data quality, stability of patterns, and the risk of oversimplifying control decisions**.

1) **Data and parameter sensitivity**
- ABC depends on correct *consumption value* (quantity × cost) and correct ranking/cumulation; errors in demand history, prices, or units can push items into the wrong class. (Lecture 5, Slide 28)  
- XYZ depends on correctly identifying “stable vs seasonal vs erratic” demand; if the data window is too short/long or contains one-off events, predictability can be misclassified. (Lecture 14, Slide 21)

2) **Classifications can become outdated quickly**
- Items can move between A/B/C when prices change or when product mix shifts; likewise they can move between X/Y/Z when markets change (promotions, new competitors, lifecycle effects). If you don’t refresh regularly, the strategy no longer matches reality. (Lecture 14, Slide 21)

3) **Oversimplification: value and predictability are not the only drivers**
- ABC/XYZ focuses on *value share* and *demand predictability*, but inventory decisions also depend on lead times, supplier risk, substitution, criticality/stockout impact, and capacity/service trade-offs—so relying on the matrix alone can mis-prioritize items. (Lecture 11, Slide 42)

4) **Risk of “wrong effort allocation” in the combined matrix**
- The combined ABC-XYZ approach is meant to tailor control effort (forecasting accuracy, safety stock, physical control) by cell. If the classification is noisy or misunderstood, you may spend too much effort on low-impact items or too little on items that actually drive service problems. (Lecture 5, Slide 35)

5) **Intermittent/erratic demand items remain hard to manage**
- Z-items are explicitly “difficult/irregular” with low forecast accuracy—so the classification tells you they’re hard, but it doesn’t solve the underlying forecasting problem; policies can default to crude buffers, which can still create either excess or stockouts. # Slide 15 of Lecture 5 contains information about The Economic Order Quantity

(EOQ) Model
The Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) model provides a way to determine the optimal order quantity by balancing different types of inventory costs. Inventory costs can be classified into purchase costs, which are the prices to be paid when buying items, order processing costs, which are the costs of procuring the inventory, and inventory holding costs, which include warehousing and related expenses. In the following notation, \(D\) represents the annual use of a particular item in number of items per annum, while \(S\) is the order-processing cost, expressed in \$/order. The parameter \(p\) denotes the price per item in \$/unit, and \(H\) stands for the holding cost per unit per year in \$/unit/year. The variable \(Q\) is the number of items ordered in one purchase order, measured in units, and \(T\) denotes the time period between purchase orders as a fraction of a year. In addition, \(SS\) is the safety stock in units, \(L\) is the lead time in fraction of a year and \(I\) is the current inventory on hand in units. Finally, TAC designates the total annual cost of the inventory system. 15

How does Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory management differ from the EOQ approach?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

JIT and EOQ are both inventory management approaches, but they’re built on different assumptions and optimize different trade-offs.

## 1) Core objective
- **JIT (Just-In-Time):** Minimize inventory by receiving/producing items *only when needed*, aiming to eliminate waste and keep stock close to zero. (Lecture 5, Slide 41; Lecture 12, Slide 30)
- **EOQ (Economic Order Quantity):** Find an *optimal batch size* \(Q\) that minimizes total annual inventory cost by balancing ordering costs and holding costs. (Lecture 5, Slide 15)

## 2) How replenishment decisions are made
- **JIT:** Replenishment is driven by *actual consumption/production sequence* (pull logic). In sequenced JIT, deliveries are synchronized to the exact production order/variant requirements. (Lecture 12, Slide 30)
- **EOQ:** Replenishment is typically planned using *fixed order quantities* (the EOQ) and ordering frequency derived from demand \(D\), order cost \(S\), and holding cost \(H\). (Lecture 5, Slide 15)

## 3) Inventory levels and buffers
- **JIT:** Tries to reduce buffers; problems are exposed quickly, so it relies heavily on stable processes, short/consistent lead times, and reliable suppliers. (Lecture 12, Slide 30)
- **EOQ:** Accepts inventory as an economic buffer; it explicitly includes/relates to concepts like cycle stock from ordering in batches and often uses **safety stock (SS)** to protect against uncertainty. (Lecture 5, Slide 15; Lecture 11, Slide 42)

## 4) When each tends to fit best (rule of thumb)
- **JIT:** Best when demand and production are predictable enough and the supply base/logistics can support frequent, reliable deliveries (especially important with high product variety in sequenced environments). (Lecture 12, Slide 30)
- **EOQ:** Best when ordering has meaningful fixed costs and holding costs matter—so you benefit from an “economic” batch size rather than very frequent small deliveries. (Lecture 5, Slide 15)

# Slide 22 of Lecture 7 contains information about Temporary Admission and Processing under Customs Control
The slide explains two different **special customs procedures** within the EU:  
**(1) Temporary Admission** and **(2) Processing under Customs Control**.  
Both involve postponing or avoiding import duties under specific conditions. The slide contains two diagrams that visually illustrate the flow of goods through each procedure.

## 1. Temporary Admission
### Text Explanation
Temporary Admission allows goods to be **used or displayed in the EU without paying import duties or taxes**, provided:
- They are imported only temporarily.
- They are **re-exported in the same state** (no substantial transformation).
- Release into free circulation is *not* intended or normally permitted under this procedure.

This procedure is commonly used for:
- Exhibition goods  
- Professional equipment  
- Goods temporarily brought in for testing or demonstration  

### Picture Description (Top Diagram)
The top diagram shows the process using symbols and flags:

1. **Importation**:  
   A good arrives from a non-EU country (shown with a Swiss flag).
2. **Temporary Admission**:  
   A box labeled “Temporary Admission” with a prohibition symbol over customs duties—meaning **no duties are paid**.
3. **Use in the EU**:  
   Goods are used or displayed inside the EU.
4. **Re-exportation**:  
   Goods leave the EU and return to the original non-EU country (Swiss flag).
5. **Prohibited release**:  
   A crossed-out EU flag and a crossed-out “Release into Free Circulation” symbol indicate that the goods **cannot** be converted into Union goods under this procedure.

The diagram emphasizes:  
**Temporary Admission = Use in EU → Re-export → No duties → No free circulation.**

## 2. Processing under Customs Control
### Text Explanation
Processing under Customs Control allows goods to undergo **processing or treatment in the EU** with:
- Postponement of duties and taxes.
- Assessment of lower duties after processing, **if the processing results in lower-value goods**  
  (example: denaturing alcohol).
This procedure enables businesses to import goods, modify them under customs supervision, and then:
- Re-export them, or  
- Release them into free circulation at a reduced duty rate based on their **processed condition**.

### Picture Description (Bottom Diagram)
1. **Importation**:  
   A product arrives from a non-EU country (example shown with a Ukrainian flag).
2. **Processing under Customs Control**:  
   A box labelled “Processing under Customs Control,” again with a symbol showing suspended duty payment.
3. **Processing in the EU**:  
   Goods undergo manufacturing, alteration, or degradation (represented by gear icons).
4. **Release into Free Circulation**:  
   A final EU flag and a symbol showing euro coins indicate that the processed goods may be **released into free circulation**, with duties calculated based on their processed form.
The diagram highlights:  
**Processing → Value modification → Free circulation allowed (with adjusted duties).**

# Overall Purpose of the Slide

The slide compares two customs regimes:
- **Temporary Admission**  
  → Goods enter the EU temporarily, no duties, must be re-exported unchanged.
- **Processing under Customs Control**  
  → Goods can be processed in the EU, and duties are assessed afterward, often at a reduced rate.
Both offer significant customs benefits but differ in their intended use and the treatment of goods.

Businesses manage safety stock effectively by treating it as a *risk buffer* (for demand and/or supply uncertainty) that is sized, positioned, and reviewed systematically—not as a fixed “extra %”.

## 1) Clarify what disruptions you are buffering against
- Separate **demand variability** (forecast error, promotions) from **supply variability** (supplier reliability, transport delays, customs holds).  
- Decide whether safety stock should protect against *short spikes* or *long interruptions*—this affects whether you need “cycle stock + safety stock” or a dedicated **contingency buffer**.

## 2) Choose the right service target and translate it into a safety stock level
- Set a **target service level** by item class (e.g., A-items higher than C-items) and by customer promise (OTIF, fill rate).  
- Then size safety stock based on variability during replenishment lead time (classic logic: more uncertainty or longer lead time ⇒ more safety stock).

## 3) Reduce the required safety stock by shortening or stabilizing lead times
Safety stock is often compensating for unstable lead times. Reduce the need by:
- Improving supplier reliability (expediting rules, capacity reservations, dual sourcing for critical items).
- Using faster/more reliable transport *selectively* when risk is high (e.g., temporary shifts to air for high-value, time-critical SKUs). Air freight prices can be volatile, so treat it as a contingency lever rather than a default (Lecture 10, Slide 28).

## 4) Place safety stock at the right point in the BOM / product structure
For assembled products, you don’t always want all buffer at the finished-goods level:
- Buffer **common components** or long-lead-time parts to protect multiple end items.
- Use requirement planning logic to see how a top-level demand translates into component gross and net requirements, and where inventory already exists (Lecture 12, Slide 12).
- This often lowers total inventory while protecting service (risk pooling on shared parts).

## 5) Link safety stock decisions to production and scheduling reality
If production/assembly capacity is a bottleneck, inventory alone may not protect customer dates.
- Use **forward vs backward scheduling** to understand whether meeting due dates is constrained by component availability or by task timing/precedence (Lecture 12, Slide 15).  
- If backward scheduling shows late starts are impossible without earlier material availability, you may need safety stock specifically on the gating components.

## 6) Make safety stock dynamic: monitor, review, and trigger actions
- Recalculate buffers periodically (monthly/quarterly) or when volatility shifts (new supplier, route changes, demand regime change).
- Set **exception triggers**: supplier OTIF drops, lead time variance rises, forecast error increases, or disruption indicators (port congestion, customs changes).
- Combine inventory buffers with *non-inventory* mitigations: alternate materials, approved second suppliers, flexible pack sizes, postponement.

## 7) Govern it with segmentation and clear ownership
- Segment SKUs (ABC/XYZ or criticality) to avoid “one rule for all.”
- Assign ownership: planning sets targets, procurement manages lead-time risk, operations confirms feasible schedules, finance validates working capital impact.

If you tell me your context (make-to-stock vs make-to-order, typical lead times, and what “disruptions” you see most—supplier delays, transport, demand spikes), I can suggest a practical safety-stock policy structure (segmentation + review cadence + triggers) tailored to that situation.

# Slide 9 of Lecture 5 contains information about Inventory Management

The purpose of inventory management is the development of relevant inventory strategies and the achievement of high inventory performance. At the same time, it aims at reducing inventory and related costs as much as possible while still maintaining responsiveness, high customer satisfaction and general operational capabilities. In order to reach these goals, several key decisions have to be made. These include determining the size of the inventory and the appropriate time of stock keeping, deciding when to reorder and what exactly triggers the decision, specifying how much to order or reorder and, finally, deciding where to locate how much inventory in the supply chain. 



[Lecture = 13] [Slide = 14]

# Slide 14 of Lecture 13 contains information about e.g. Supply Chain Relation Spectrum
In the supply chain relation spectrum (see lesson 3), the green arrow describes increasing complexity and sophistication of several important elements. As collaboration deepens, **information systems**, **systems infrastructure**, **decision support systems**, **planning mechanisms**, **information sharing** and **process understanding** all become more advanced and more tightly integrated. Moreover, higher levels of collaboration imply that both trading partners need to have equivalent, or at least close, levels of supply chain maturity in order for the relationship to function effectively. At the most advanced end, **synchronized collaboration** demands joint planning, shared R&D and extensive sharing of information and processing models, leading to movement towards real‑time customer demand information throughout the supply chain and across a range of relationships. This spectrum of collaboration, adapted from Cohen and Roussel (Slide 14), ranges from **transactional**, **cooperative**, and **coordinated** relationships up to **synchronized relationships**, and it also reflects the **extent of collaboration**—from limited relationships with low return to extensive but potentially not viable arrangements—as well as the **number of relationships**, moving from many to few, as captured in Strategy & Configuration.



[Lecture = 13] [Slide = 17]

# Slide 17 of Lecture 13 contains information about SCM – e.g. Simchi Levi’s Key Issues
Simchi‑Levi highlights several key issues in supply chain management and links each **issue** to important **considerations**. Under **network planning**, managers must decide on warehouse locations and capacities, plant locations and production levels, and transportation flows between facilities so as to minimize cost and time. With respect to **inventory control**, they need to ask how inventory should be managed, why inventory fluctuates, and which strategies can minimize these fluctuations. For **supply contracts**, the impact of volume discounts and revenue sharing has to be evaluated, along with pricing strategies designed to reduce order‑shipment variability. When thinking about **distribution strategies**, firms must choose between options such as direct ship versus cross‑docking, determine how many cross‑dock points are needed, and assess the costs and benefits of different strategies. In the area of **integration and strategic partnering**, it becomes crucial to ask how integration with partners can be achieved, what level of integration is best, what information and processes can be shared, and which partnerships should be implemented in which situations. Regarding **outsourcing and procurement strategies**, companies must identify which capabilities are core to the supply chain and which are not, whether product design requires different outsourcing approaches, and how to address risk management. Finally, **product design** raises questions about how inventory holding and transportation costs are affected by design choices, and how product design can enable mass customization. All of these key issues and considerations are brought together in Strategy & Configuration Slide 17.

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
In what ways can supply chain collaboration among suppliers, manufacturers, and retailers improve inventory management outcomes?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Supply chain collaboration improves inventory management because it changes **how decisions are made (jointly rather than locally)** and **what information those decisions are based on (shared rather than siloed)**—which directly affects reorder timing, order quantities, and inventory placement across the chain. (Lecture 5, Slide 9)

### 1) Better demand visibility → less “buffering” and lower safety stocks
- When retailers share POS sales, promotions, and forecast updates with upstream partners, suppliers and manufacturers rely less on “guesses” and less on inflated orders as a proxy for demand.
- This reduces inventory held “just in case,” while maintaining responsiveness and service. (Lecture 5, Slide 9)
- It also addresses the core question of *why inventory fluctuates* and how to reduce that fluctuation. (Lecture 13, Slide 17)

### 2) Coordinated replenishment decisions → fewer stockouts and fewer excesses
Collaboration supports aligning key inventory decisions:
- **When to reorder / what triggers replenishment** (e.g., shared reorder points or shared event triggers like promotions)
- **How much to order** (e.g., coordinated batch sizes, smoother ordering patterns)
- **Where to hold inventory** (e.g., shifting stock upstream/downstream based on who can respond fastest) (Lecture 5, Slide 9)

This improves inventory performance outcomes (availability, responsiveness) while controlling cost. (Lecture 5, Slide 9)

### 3) Joint planning mechanisms and integrated systems → faster, higher-quality decisions
As relationships move from transactional to coordinated/synchronized collaboration, partners invest in:
- more integrated **information systems and infrastructure**
- stronger **planning mechanisms** and **decision support**
- deeper **information sharing** and shared process understanding (Lecture 13, Slide 14)

These capabilities enable quicker replanning when demand or supply changes—reducing the need for large inventories as “shock absorbers.” (Lecture 13, Slide 14; Lecture 5, Slide 9)

### 4) Contract and incentive alignment → reduced order variability (bullwhip)
Collaboration often includes adjusting commercial terms (e.g., pricing schemes, volume discounts, revenue sharing) to discourage large, infrequent, or speculative ordering.
- The goal is explicitly to **reduce order–shipment variability**, which is a major driver of unnecessary inventory and poor service. (Lecture 13, Slide 17)

### 5) Network-wide inventory positioning → system-level cost/service improvement
When manufacturers, suppliers, and retailers collaborate, inventory placement becomes a *network planning* question, not just a local warehouse/store decision:
- deciding how inventory should be distributed across facilities and flows to minimize total cost and time (Lecture 13, Slide 17)
- directly linked to deciding **where to locate how much inventory in the supply chain** (Lecture 5, Slide 9)

### 6) Shared understanding of inventory trade-offs → clearer, aligned targets
Collaboration helps partners agree on the trade-offs between:
- service level, lead time, capacity, and inventory
- and on which control approaches (EOQ, safety stock, reorder tactics, selective strategies like ABC/XYZ) fit different items and contexts. (Lecture 11, Slide 42)

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What criteria should companies consider when selecting an outsourcing partner for their supply chain needs?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

When selecting an outsourcing partner (supplier/3PL/contract manufacturer) for supply chain activities, you should build a **multi-criteria evaluation**—not just compare unit prices—because the “best” partner depends on service, risk, and long-term strategic fit as well as cost. (Lecture 6, Slide 23)

### 1) Start with “order qualifiers” (must-haves)
These are the baseline requirements a partner must meet to even be considered:
- **On-time delivery reliability** and **dependability of supply** (Lecture 6, Slide 23; Lecture 11, Slide 25)  
- **Quality conformance** and relevant **quality certifications** (Lecture 6, Slide 23; Lecture 11, Slide 25)  
- **Lead time** performance (Lecture 6, Slide 23)  
- Ability to supply the **required quantity** and offer **delivery/volume flexibility** (Lecture 11, Slide 25)  
- **Financial and managerial capability** / stability (Lecture 6, Slide 23; Lecture 11, Slide 25)

### 2) Evaluate “total cost,” not just price
Compare suppliers on the **total cost of being supplied** (e.g., all relevant cost elements across the relationship), and treat price as only one input in the decision. (Lecture 11, Slide 25; Lecture 6, Slide 23)

### 3) Check responsiveness and uncertainty-handling
A strong outsourcing partner should handle variability:
- **Responsiveness to demand uncertainty** and operational agility (Lecture 6, Slide 23)  
- **Responsiveness** as a service capability (Lecture 11, Slide 25)

### 4) Assess track record and relationship fit
Go beyond today’s performance and check:
- **Performance history/track record** (Lecture 6, Slide 23)  
- **Ease of doing business** (processes, communication, coordination) (Lecture 11, Slide 25)  
- **Senior management attitude/commitment** to the relationship (Lecture 6, Slide 23)  
- **Willingness to share risk** and **long-term commitment** to supply (Lecture 11, Slide 25)

### 5) Screen longer-term capabilities (strategic potential)
If the outsourced activity is important for competitiveness, prioritize partners who can grow with you:
- **Innovation potential** (Lecture 11, Slide 25)  
- **Knowledge transfer** capability (not only delivering a service, but helping you improve) (Lecture 11, Slide 25)  
- Strong **technical, operations, and process capabilities** (Lecture 11, Slide 25)

### 6) Include sustainability/CSR and compliance
Many firms now treat this as a core requirement:
- **Corporate social responsibility (CSR) record** and broader compliance expectations (Lecture 6, Slide 23)

### 7) Turn criteria into a structured decision
A practical approach is to:
1) Define must-haves (qualifiers),  
2) Weight the remaining criteria (cost, service, risk, innovation, CSR),  
3) Score suppliers using both quantitative and qualitative inputs, and  
4) Select the partner that best matches your supply chain priorities. (Lecture 6, Slide 29; Lecture 11, Slide 25)

If you tell me what you’re outsourcing (e.g., warehousing, transport, customer service, manufacturing) and your main goal (cost, speed, flexibility, risk reduction), I can help you tailor a weighted criteria set.

There are also different levels to consider: supply chain level, company level and process level. It is no longer all about technology, warehouses, distribution centres, trucks or planes.

At the supply chain level (a global view), the supply chain is any combination of processes, functions, activities, relationships and pathways along which products, services, information and financial transactions move in and between enterprises. # Slide 24 of Lecture 11 contains information about Kraljik matrix
The Kraljik matrix distinguishes different types of suppliers according to their impact on financial results and the level of supply risk. At a high impact on financial results, leverage suppliers are characterised by many competitors and commodity products, while strategic suppliers are market leaders with specific know‑how, and in this area the balance of power may differ among buyer and supplier. At a lower impact or with a focus on more routine and bottleneck situations, routine suppliers are associated with large supply and many suppliers with a dependent position, whereas bottleneck suppliers are technology leaders with few, if any, alternative suppliers, which may lead to a supplier‑dominated segment where it is advisable to reduce the number of suppliers. Overall, the Kraljik matrix spans low to high supply risk and low to high supplier impact on financial results to position leverage, strategic, routine and bottleneck suppliers.

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
How can technology and data analytics improve the supplier selection process in the supply chain?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Technology and data analytics improve supplier selection by making the process (1) more evidence-based, (2) faster to run and update, and (3) better aligned with the supply chain’s end-to-end objectives and risk profile.

## 1) Start from an end-to-end view of what “good” means
Before choosing tools, define the selection goals across material, information, and financial flows—because supplier performance affects the whole chain, not just purchasing price. This ensures you evaluate suppliers on what improves coordination and competitive advantage, not only on isolated KPIs. (Lecture 1, Slide 37; Lecture 2, Slide 9)

**Practical step:** translate strategy into a scorecard (cost, service, flexibility, innovation, risk, etc.) and decide which criteria matter most for this category.

## 2) Use analytics to structure and quantify multi-criteria decisions
Supplier selection typically involves many criteria—some “static” (quality, dependability, total cost, volume flexibility) and some “dynamic” (innovation potential, risk sharing, long-term commitment, technical/operations capabilities). Data analytics helps you:
- measure each criterion consistently (e.g., delivery reliability from OTIF data; quality from defect rates; responsiveness from lead-time variance),
- combine them into an overall supplier rating using weighted scoring,
- run sensitivity analyses to see how robust the ranking is if weights or assumptions change. (Lecture 11, Slide 25)

**Practical step:** build a simple weighted scoring model, then test “what if quality weight increases?” or “what if lead times become more volatile?”

## 3) Improve cost evaluation with “total cost-to-serve” and predictive cost drivers
Instead of comparing only unit prices, analytics can estimate *total cost of being supplied* by integrating:
- logistics and handling costs,
- inventory costs (driven by lead time and variability),
- quality failure costs (returns, rework),
- expediting and disruption costs. (Lecture 11, Slide 25)

**Practical step:** use historical purchase orders, freight invoices, and quality claims to quantify cost drivers per supplier.

## 4) Make risk visible using data and the Kraljic perspective
Technology enables better assessment of supply risk and supplier impact (financial importance), which is exactly the logic behind segmenting suppliers (routine/leverage/bottleneck/strategic). With better data, you can place suppliers more accurately and choose an appropriate sourcing approach (e.g., dual-sourcing for bottlenecks, partnership focus for strategic). (Lecture 11, Slide 24)

**Practical step:** define risk indicators (single-site dependency, financial health signals, lead-time volatility, capacity constraints) and use them to support your Kraljic positioning.

## 5) Capture qualitative insights in a consistent way (not “gut feel”)
Many important criteria are qualitative—ease of doing business, willingness to share risk, long-term commitment, innovation. Digital tools (supplier relationship management platforms, structured surveys, standardized evaluation templates) help convert these into consistent ratings and reduce bias across evaluators. (Lecture 11, Slide 25)

**Practical step:** have cross-functional stakeholders (procurement, operations, quality, R&D) score the same rubric and reconcile differences.

## 6) Enable continuous supplier selection (not a one-off event)
With integrated data flows, you can re-evaluate supplier performance continuously—so the “best supplier” reflects current realities (service trends, risk changes), not last year’s tender.

**Practical step:** set thresholds and alerts (e.g., if OTIF drops below X or lead-time variance rises above Y, trigger a re-assessment).

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
How can companies measure the success of their buyer-supplier relationships in the context of outsourcing?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

To measure whether a buyer–supplier relationship is “successful” in outsourcing, it helps to evaluate it from multiple angles (performance, cost, risk, and relationship fit), not just price. Here’s a structured way to do it.

## 1) Define what “success” means for *this* outsourced activity
Start by clarifying the intended value: is the goal cost reduction, access to capabilities, scalability, speed, or quality? This links your measures to the outsourcing rationale and avoids optimizing the wrong KPI. (Lecture 14, Slide 22; Lecture 11, Slide 43)

## 2) Match metrics to the *type of relationship* you want
Use the idea that low strategic-importance purchases typically suit arm’s-length relationships, while high strategic-importance purchases require more collaborative partnerships/alliances. Then measure success accordingly (transactional compliance vs. joint improvement/innovation). (Lecture 3, Slide 37)

- **Arm’s-length (vendor/traditional supplier):** focus on efficiency and compliance (OTD, defects, invoice accuracy).
- **Collaborative (partnership/strategic alliance):** add metrics for joint value creation (innovation contributions, responsiveness in disruptions, continuous improvement results).

## 3) Track operational delivery performance (hard service outcomes)
Create a small dashboard of core service KPIs tied to the outsourced scope:
- **Delivery:** late delivery rate / on-time-in-full
- **Quality:** quality consistency, defect/rework, “mistakes”
- **Service execution:** responsiveness, reliability, need for frequent reminders
These directly reflect common failure drivers in outsourcing relationships—so improvements here are strong signals of relationship success. (Lecture 6, Slide 21)

## 4) Measure relationship health and coordination effectiveness (soft-but-measurable)
Outsourcing often fails due to coordination frictions; measure them explicitly:
- **Communication quality** (e.g., issue-resolution time, escalation frequency)
- **Supplier commitment** (e.g., attendance/preparedness in governance meetings, follow-through on action plans)
- **Cultural/time-zone friction indicators** (e.g., handover delays, misunderstandings, rework due to misalignment)
These are repeatedly cited problem areas and are practical leading indicators before operational KPIs degrade. (Lecture 6, Slide 21)

## 5) Evaluate cost outcomes using “total cost,” not only price
Assess whether outsourcing is delivering the expected economics by using **Total Cost of Ownership** logic: include coordination/management effort, quality costs, expediting, switching costs, etc.—not just the contracted rate. This gives a truer read of whether the relationship is actually successful. (Lecture 14, Slide 22; Lecture 6, Slide 2)

## 6) Monitor risk, compliance, and trust-related outcomes
Because outsourcing shifts boundaries, success should include risk control:
- **Confidentiality / IP incidents**
- **Customer complaints linked to supplier performance**
- **Compliance and audit performance**
These map directly to commonly reported outsourcing problems and protect long-term value. (Lecture 6, Slide 21)

## 7) Put governance in place and review performance jointly
Use a recurring review cycle (monthly/quarterly) where you:
1) review KPI trends (steps 3–6),
2) identify root causes,
3) agree improvement actions and owners.
This reinforces the “right” relationship type (arm’s-length vs collaborative) and makes success measurable over time. (Lecture 3, Slide 37; Lecture 14, Slide 22)

# Slide 15 of Lecture 6 contains information about Total Cost of Ownership – Cost Elements and Cost Drivers

### Column Definitions
**Activity Related to the Purchasing Process** describes the stage of the purchasing process (pretransaction, transaction, posttransaction) and the specific activity performed.

**Potential Cost Elements** lists the types of costs that arise from each activity (e.g., capital requisition, price paid, downtime).

**Cost Drivers** explains the underlying factors that cause or influence those costs (e.g., labor, documents, equipment movement).

---

## Row-by-Row Description

### PRETRANSACTION

**Row: Need for new production equipment identified**  
Activity: Identifying the need for new equipment.  
Potential Cost Elements: Capital requisition; form committee to investigate.  
Cost Drivers: Creating and filing documents; salaries of committee members.

**Row: Form design team**  
Activity: Creating a team to evaluate and design solutions.  
Potential Cost Elements: Team costs; identifying external candidates such as potential suppliers.  
Cost Drivers: Salaries of team members; costs of identifying, contacting, and meeting candidates.

---

### TRANSACTION

**Row: Equipment Purchased**  
Activity: Buying the equipment.  
Potential Cost Elements: Price paid.  
Cost Drivers: Cost of equipment; delivery; warranty.

**Row: Equipment Installation**  
Activity: Installing the equipment.  
Potential Cost Elements: Installing equipment; shutting down other operations.  
Cost Drivers: Labor, moving old equipment, raw materials, losses from destroyed/tested items, finished goods shortages, and labor if paid for idle time.

---

### POSTTRANSACTION

**Row: Routine Maintenance**  
Activity: Conducting regular maintenance.  
Potential Cost Elements: Downtime; cost of warranty or out-of-warranty work.  
Cost Drivers: Labor downtime; inventory buildup or shortages; price paid for work performed.

**Row: Repairs**  
Activity: Repairing the equipment after issues arise.  
Potential Cost Elements: Downtime; cost of warranty or out-of-warranty work.  
Cost Drivers: Labor downtime; inventory buildup or shortages; price paid for repair work.

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What role does logistics play in determining the Total Cost of Ownership in supply chain procurement?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Logistics matters in TCO because it makes many costs visible beyond the supplier’s unit price—especially in the **transaction** and **posttransaction** phases—and those costs can be large enough to change which supplier is “best” in a procurement decision. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)

### 1) Start from the TCO logic: price is only one transaction element
In the TCO breakdown, **delivery/transportation** sits alongside price, ordering, tariffs/duties, billing, inspection, returns, and follow-up. So logistics is explicitly a *core* part of the “cost to buy,” not an add-on. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)

### 2) Transaction-phase logistics costs (direct, often measurable)
When comparing suppliers, logistics typically affects these TCO components:
- **Delivery/transportation**: freight rates, accessorial charges, packaging/handling, insurance, expediting. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)  
- **Tariffs/duties**: driven by cross-border flows and Incoterms/route choices—logistics decisions influence the landed cost. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)  
- **Inspection and returns**: logistics affects how costly and slow it is to inspect inbound goods and to return parts (reverse logistics). (Lecture 6, Slide 14)

### 3) Posttransaction logistics costs (indirect, often underestimated)
Logistics performance (lead time reliability, damage rates, responsiveness) drives downstream costs such as:
- **Line fallout / downtime** if materials arrive late or unusable, causing production interruptions. (Lecture 6, Slide 14; Lecture 6, Slide 15)  
- **Field failures, repair/replacement in the field, and spare parts/maintenance costs**—logistics affects service parts availability and the cost/speed of getting technicians/parts to the customer. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)  
- **Customer goodwill/reputation impacts** when delivery failures or service delays affect the customer experience. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)

### 4) Pretransaction logistics implications (set-up and integration work)
Before buying, logistics-related work can appear in activities like **qualifying sources** and **educating the supplier/firm in each other’s operations**—e.g., aligning delivery schedules, labeling, EDI, packaging specs, and inbound processes. Those are real set-up costs in TCO. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)

### 5) How to use this in procurement decisions (practical approach)
To reflect logistics in TCO, you’d:
1. Map the supplier’s flow across **pre/transaction/post** phases. (Lecture 6, Slide 14)  
2. List logistics-touching cost elements (transport, duties, inspection/returns, downtime/service impacts). (Lecture 6, Slide 14; Lecture 6, Slide 15)  
3. Identify the **cost drivers** (e.g., distance, variability, handling complexity, installation downtime) to compare suppliers on more than unit price. (Lecture 6, Slide 15)

# Slide 4 of Lecture 7 contains information about Legal Framework of Trade

The legal framework of trade is formed by norms and rules of international law and multinational treaties or agreements, which together build up a supra-national legal framework. This includes organisations and regimes such as the UNO, OECD, EEC/EC/EU and GATT/WTO, as well as bilateral commercial treaties and trade agreements. Alongside these, national regulations—mainly following national or regional interests—also play a major role, including external trade law and customs law. Furthermore, Lex Mercatoria encompasses national and multinational regulations that allow valid cross-border legal transactions and their enforcement. International procedural law and the law of sales contracts, together with regulations about cross-border enforcement of sentences, provide additional structure. Mediation and international arbitration offer alternatives to ordinary court litigation procedures in resolving cross-border trade disputes. 4

What are some best practices for companies to adopt in order to navigate the complexities of trade facilitation?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

To navigate trade facilitation effectively, companies should treat it as a mix of (1) rules/procedures, (2) information and systems, (3) day-to-day customs management, and (4) governance to keep improvements in place. A practical set of best practices aligned with these four areas is:

1) Simplify and harmonize your internal trade processes  
- Standardize export/import workflows across business units (clear SOPs for classification, valuation, origin, documentation, and record-keeping) so the same “rules and procedures” are applied consistently. (Lecture 7, Slide 8)  
- Create a reusable “document and data checklist” per lane/product to reduce errors and rework at borders—think of it as internal harmonization mirroring external harmonization. (Lecture 7, Slide 8)

2) Modernize trade data management and information sharing  
- Invest in strong master data (product descriptions, HS codes, supplier/customer details) and ensure “single source of truth” data flows into customs filings, invoices, and logistics documents to support smoother information lodging with authorities and partners. (Lecture 7, Slide 8)  
- Improve collaboration between functions (sales, logistics, finance, legal) and with external stakeholders (forwarders, customs brokers) so information is shared early and consistently—especially when changes occur (e.g., supplier change, routing change). (Lecture 7, Slide 8)

3) Strengthen customs and trade compliance execution (“administration & management”)  
- Build a compliance operating rhythm: pre-shipment checks for sensitive lanes/products, post-entry audits, and periodic reviews of broker performance and customs outcomes (holds, penalties, lead times). (Lecture 7, Slide 8)  
- Develop internal expertise (or a clear partnership model with brokers) on export/import operations—i.e., know what you need to manage in practice, not just in principle. (Lecture 7, Slide 2)

4) Put governance and institutional mechanisms in place  
- Assign clear ownership: a trade compliance lead and defined roles/responsibilities across the organization so implementation doesn’t depend on individuals and is sustained over time. (Lecture 7, Slide 8)  
- Use formal dispute-resolution and contracting practices for cross-border trade (e.g., aligning sales contracts, procedures, and escalation paths) to reduce uncertainty when issues arise. This sits within the wider legal framework and enforcement mechanisms shaping international trade. (Lecture 7, Slide 4)

5) Use trade terms (Incoterms) strategically to reduce friction and risk  
- Choose Incoterms that match your operational capability and risk appetite (who arranges transport, insurance, export/import clearance). Misaligned Incoterms often create delays, unexpected costs, or compliance gaps. (Lecture 7, Slide 2; Lecture 11, Slide 44)

# Slide 48 of Lecture 2 contains information about Incoterms -Understanding
Incoterms are published by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC). They constitute a set of rules for the interpretation of commonly used international commercial terms (INCOTERMS). First published by the ICC in 1936, they have since been updated in 1953, 1967, 1976, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010 and, most recently, in 2020. # Slide 34 of Lecture 7 contains information about Incoterms®

Trade Terms
Trade terms can be industry‑specific contract terms or regional usages that are interpreted differently from place to place or from country to country. International commercial terms, or Incoterms®, provide a common and widely accepted set of standardised trade terms. First introduced in 1936 by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) in Paris, Incoterms® have been revised several times, with the latest revision being Incoterms® 2020. They deal with the obligations of buyer and seller arising from a sales contract and with the apportionment of the costs and risks associated with the movement of goods. Incoterms® can be divided into four groups: Group E (Ex‑Works), Group F (movement of goods arranged by the buyer), Group C (movement of goods arranged by the seller) and Group D (goods delivered). 34

# Slide 37 of Lecture 7 contains information about Further Main Characteristics

Further main characteristics of Incoterms® include the distinction between one‑point and two‑point clauses. One‑point clauses, in which the transfer of risks and costs occurs at the same place, include EXW, FCA, FAS, FOB, DAP, DPU and DDP. Two‑point clauses, where the place of transfer of risk and the place of transfer of costs differ, include CPT, CIP, CFR and CIF.  
Certain Incoterms® are principally applicable for any mode or modes of transport, such as EXW, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU and DDP. Others—FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF—are intended only for maritime shipping and inland waterways, where goods are delivered on board or alongside a vessel in a port, and they are not recommended for container transports. Incoterms® can be used for international as well as domestic shipments and can accommodate arrangements for carriage with either the seller’s or the buyer’s own means of transport in FCA, DAP, DPU and DDP. They have to be explicitly incorporated into a sales contract, for example by stating “[…] according to Incoterms® 2020”, and the “named place” has to be specified as precisely as possible, for instance by using a postal address or a UN/LOCODE (`http://www.unece.org/cefact/locode/welcome.html/`). 37

# Slide 63 of Lecture 2 contains information about Incoterms – Purpose and Scope
In pricing terms, shipping terms and sales terms, Incoterms define the rights and obligations of the parties to the contract of sale with respect to the delivery of goods sold. They clarify how functions, costs and risks are split between buyer and seller for the delivery of goods, as required by the sales contract.

As you move from group “E” to “D”, the seller's risk and cost on the cargo increase, while the buyer’s risk and cost on the cargo decrease.

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What are some common misconceptions about Incoterms® 2020 that businesses should be aware of?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Common misconceptions come from treating Incoterms® as “the whole contract” rather than a *delivery-rule* that allocates tasks, costs, and risk at defined points. Here are several to watch for:

1) **“Incoterms® cover everything in the deal.”**  
Incoterms® mainly clarify the *obligations of buyer/seller* and the *split of costs and risks* linked to moving goods under the sales contract—not payment terms, product quality, liability for defects, dispute resolution, etc. (Lecture 7, Slide 34; Lecture 2, Slide 63)

2) **“Risk and cost always transfer at the same point.”**  
Some terms are *two‑point clauses*, where risk transfers at one place but costs are borne to a later place. For example, CFR/CIF are classic cases where the seller pays carriage further, but risk transfers earlier. This surprises firms that assume “who pays freight = who bears risk.” (Lecture 7, Slide 37)

3) **“FOB/CIF are fine for container shipping because everyone uses them.”**  
FOB/FAS/CFR/CIF are intended for maritime/inland waterway shipments where delivery is on/alongside the vessel in a port, and they are **not recommended for container transport** (where handover typically happens before the goods are loaded on the ship). Misuse can create gaps in who controls/insures the goods at handover. (Lecture 7, Slide 37)

4) **“CIF means the seller carries the risk to destination.”**  
Under CIF (and CFR), the seller may pay costs deep into the journey, but **risk still transfers earlier** (similar risk point as FOB/CFR/CIF in the sea-terms overview). Businesses often confuse “seller pays” with “seller is at risk.” (Lecture 2, Slide 51; Lecture 7, Slide 37)

5) **“Incoterms® automatically apply if we write FOB/CIF in an email.”**  
They must be explicitly incorporated into the sales contract and referenced to the ruleset (e.g., “Incoterms® 2020”). Otherwise, parties may interpret the term using local trade usage or prior versions, leading to disputes. (Lecture 7, Slide 37; Lecture 7, Slide 34)

6) **“The ‘named place’ isn’t that important.”**  
The *named place* is critical because it anchors where delivery/risk/cost responsibilities apply. Vague places (e.g., “Copenhagen”) can cause arguments about which terminal/port/address is meant. Best practice is specifying very precisely (address/terminal/UN‑LOCODE). (Lecture 7, Slide 37)

7) **“All Incoterms® work the same way; choosing one is just price level.”**  
Moving from Group E toward Group D generally increases the seller’s cost/risk and reduces the buyer’s—so the term materially changes operational responsibilities, not just the invoice price. (Lecture 2, Slide 63; Lecture 7, Slide 34)

# Slide 29 of Lecture 10 contains information about Transport and Communication Flows along a Transport Chain

This slide ilustrates the complex network of transport and communication flows that occur along an international transport chain, showing the relationships and information exchanges between all parties involved in moving goods from an exporter to an importer across international borders.At the foundation of the diagram are the physical movement actors arranged in sequential order from left to right. The flow begins with the Exporter or Shipper, who initiates the shipment. The goods then move through a Carrier on Pre-Carriage, which represents the initial transport segment from the shipper's location to the first terminal. This is followed by the Terminal at home, which serves as a consolidation and transfer point in the origin country. From there, the Carrier on Main Haul takes responsibility for the primary transportation segment, typically the longest distance portion of the journey whether by ocean vessel, aircraft, or other long-distance mode. Upon arrival in the destination country, goods pass through the Terminal abroad, another consolidation and transfer point. Finally, the Carrier on Onward-Carriage completes the delivery to the Importer or Consignee at the final destination.Above this physical layer of actors, the diagram shows intermediary service providers who coordinate and facilitate the movement. The Freight Forwarder at home and Freight Forwarder abroad are positioned centrally and highlighted with red circles to emphasize their pivotal coordinating role. Between them sits the Transportation Broker or Agent, who may facilitate connections between the various parties. These freight forwarding entities serve as orchestrators of the entire transport chain, managing documentation, booking cargo space, coordinating transfers, and ensuring compliance with regulations.The customs authorities are represented in the upper middle section of the diagram. Customs at home handles export clearance procedures, while Customs abroad manages import clearance and duty collection. These regulatory entities interact with both the freight forwarders and, when necessary, directly with the shippers and consignees.At the top of the diagram, the Bank of Exporter and Bank of Importer are connected by a bidirectional arrow, representing the financial flows that underpin international trade. These institutions manage letters of credit, documentary collections, and payment transfers that ensure the exporter receives payment and the importer receives title to the goods.The arrows throughout the diagram indicate the direction and complexity of information and communication flows. The freight forwarders show extensive connectivity, with arrows linking them to customs authorities, transportation carriers at each stage, terminals, and the banking institutions. This reflects their role as information hubs, receiving booking instructions, issuing bills of lading, preparing customs documentation, coordinating vessel or flight schedules, and managing the flow of trade documents that accompany physical cargo.The exporter and importer also maintain direct connections with their respective banks, customs authorities, and freight forwarders, though they typically do not communicate directly with all the individual carriers and terminals. This separation of responsibilities allows shippers to focus on their core business while relying on logistics specialists to manage the operational complexity of international transport.

Source: Kummer and Schramm (2004), Kummer et al. (2010)

# Slide 43 of Lecture 12 contains information about Eg. Chain of Events – Tracking in Transportation
# Description of the Transportation Tracking Flow on the Slide 43 of lecture 12

The slide illustrates how **digital tracking** works across the entire transportation chain using **barcode or RFID scanning** at each event point.  
It shows how each status update is captured, stored in a central system, and then made available to shippers and receivers.

---

## 1. **Pickup → Short Haul → Sending Depot**
The process begins with pickup by a courier.

At **pickup**, a barcode or RFID tag is scanned, creating the first event:
- **Pickup**

The shipment then travels via short-haul truck to the **sending depot**, where additional scans occur:
- **V-NI In** (vehicle inbound)  
- **V-NI Out** (vehicle outbound)

These scans confirm that the parcel entered and left the depot.

---

## 2. **Sending Depot → Long Distance Transport → Hub**
A long-distance truck picks up consolidated shipments.

At various points:
- **Hub-In** → scanned upon arrival at the transshipment hub  
- **Hub-Out** → scanned when leaving the hub  

Every transition is logged.

The hub cross-docking step ensures the shipment is sorted for onward transport.

---

## 3. **Hub → Long Haul → Receiver Depot**
The shipment travels again via long-haul truck to the receiver's depot.

Scans include:
- **E-NI In** (entry at receiver depot)  
- **E-NI Out** (exit from receiver depot)

This ensures the item is accounted for before final delivery preparation.

---

## 4. **Receiver Depot → Short Haul → Final Delivery**
The last-mile process involves another short-haul truck dropping the shipment at the final customer.

A final scan event:
- **Delivery**

confirms the arrival.

---

## 5. **Central Event Database**
At the center of the diagram is a **database system** where all event scans are recorded.  
Each scan triggers a status update that is stored and time-stamped:
- Pickup  
- V-NI In  
- V-NI Out  
- Hub-In  
- Hub-Out  
- E-NI In  
- E-NI Out  
- Delivery  

A checklist visual shows which events have been completed.

---

## 6. **Reporting & Visibility**
Information from the central system is sent to:
- **Shippers** (who want to monitor outbound shipments)  
- **Receivers** (who monitor inbound shipments)

Real-time tracking enables:
- Exception handling  
- ETA visibility  
- Customer notifications  
- Proof of process completion  

---

## 7. **Overall Logic**
The slide demonstrates **end-to-end digital traceability**, where:
- **Every movement** of the shipment  
- **Every change in custody**  
- **Every transition between logistical steps**  

is captured through **barcode/RFID event scanning**.

These event triggers control and update the logistics chain, enabling complete transparency and better coordination.

---

## 8. **Key Message**
**Digitization of events enables full tracking and control across the logistics chain — from pickup to delivery — through standardized information points and automated status updates.**

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
What is the significance of a certificate of origin in international trade agreements?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

A **certificate of origin (CO)** is significant in international trade agreements because it is the key document used to **prove where a product “originates”** under the applicable **rules of origin**—and that proof determines which trade agreement benefits (if any) the shipment can claim.

### 1) It enables preferential tariff treatment (lower/zero duties)
Most Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) offer reduced duties **only if** the goods meet the agreement’s origin rules. The CO (or an “origin declaration” in some systems) is the practical evidence customs uses to grant those preferential rates. If you can’t prove origin, customs will typically apply the **normal (MFN) duty rate** instead. (Lecture 7, Slide 8)

### 2) It supports customs compliance and reduces clearance risk
Rules of origin are part of the WTO framework (Agreement on Rules of Origin), and customs authorities rely on origin evidence to administer trade measures consistently. A CO helps avoid delays, re-assessments, penalties, or retroactive duty claims if customs questions eligibility. (Lecture 7, Slide 8)

### 3) It determines eligibility for trade policy measures beyond tariffs
Origin is also used to apply or avoid measures such as:
- quotas and tariff-rate quotas,
- anti-dumping/countervailing duties,
- embargoes/sanctions and other restrictions,
- labeling/marking requirements in some markets.

So the CO affects not only *how much* duty you pay, but sometimes *whether you can import at all* under certain regimes. (Lecture 7, Slide 8)

### 4) It creates a standardized “language” for trade documentation
International trade facilitation bodies work on standardization of trade documents and data elements so that parties and customs can interpret information consistently across borders—origin data is one of the most important standardized elements in that documentation flow. (Lecture 7, Slide 8)

# Slide 26 of Lecture 10 contains information about Further Development of Eurasian Railway - ERAI U-West

This slide tracks the development of Eurasian Railway freight rates from July 2016 through January 2025, displaying multiple route pricing indicators measured in US dollars per forty-foot equivalent unit. The data shows six different rate series including the ERAI Composite index, ERAI U-East and U-West routes, Shanghai to Rotterdam rates in both directions, and TAC Hong Kong to Europe per ton rates.
The visualization reveals several distinct periods of market behavior. From mid-2016 through early 2020, rates remained relatively stable across all measured routes, clustering between approximately 2,000 and 4,000 USD per FEU. This period, circled in red on the chart with a notation of "2016", represents the baseline operational environment for Eurasian rail freight before major disruptions occurred.
The stability was dramatically interrupted beginning in late 2020 and extending through 2021 and into early 2022. The Shanghai to Rotterdam route, represented by the dark blue line, experienced the most extreme volatility, spiking to over 15,000 USD per FEU at its peak. The TAC Hong Kong to Europe rates shown in light blue also surged significantly, reaching approximately 8,000 USD per FEU. These sharp increases coincided with global supply chain disruptions during the pandemic period when ocean freight capacity constraints and port congestion drove shippers to seek alternative routing options through rail corridors.
Following the peaks in 2021 and early 2022, rates began a sustained decline back toward historical norms. By late 2022 and into 2023, most routes had returned to the 2,000 to 3,000 USD per FEU range. However, another period of volatility emerged in 2024, circled in red on the right side of the chart, where the Shanghai to Rotterdam rates again climbed to around 9,000 USD per FEU before declining and then experiencing renewed upward pressure.
The most recent data point highlighted on the chart indicates that as of January 2025, rates stand at 3,373 USD per FEU, suggesting a return to more normalized market conditions compared to the extreme volatility of previous years. The ERAI Composite and directional indices have remained relatively flat throughout the entire period shown, maintaining their positions in the 2,500 to 3,000 USD per FEU range with minimal deviation.
From a supply chain analytics perspective, this chart illustrates several critical concepts. The dramatic rate volatility demonstrates the intermodal competition and substitution effects between ocean and rail freight, where capacity constraints in one mode drive demand and pricing in alternative modes. The differential behavior between composite indices and specific lane rates shows how aggregated market indicators can mask significant route-level volatility. The cyclical pattern of disruption, recovery, normalization, and renewed disruption reflects the complex interplay of geopolitical events, infrastructure capacity, demand fluctuations, and competitive dynamics in transcontinental freight markets. Understanding these patterns is essential for freight procurement strategy, modal selection decisions, and supply chain risk management in global logistics operations.

How can businesses effectively integrate their online and offline channels in an omni-channel approach?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

To integrate online and offline channels effectively in an omni-channel approach, think of it as moving from “separate channels” to “one business with many touchpoints,” with inventory, data, and fulfillment working as one system.

### 1) Start with the target experience: “one brand, one journey”
Map the customer journey so customers can move seamlessly between store, web, app, etc., without hitting “breaks” in service (e.g., inconsistent prices, returns rules, or stock visibility). The omni-channel goal is that customers experience a unified brand rather than distinct channels. (Lecture 3, Slide 45)

### 2) Integrate inventory into a single view (the foundation)
Omni-channel requires coherent, absolute inventory integration across online and offline—meaning you manage stock as a shared pool rather than store stock vs. e-commerce stock. This enables promises like “see store availability online,” ship-from-store, and click-and-collect. (Lecture 8, Slide 8)

### 3) Break down operational silos and align processes
A common barrier is that even if customers see multiple touchpoints, the retailer’s operations and knowledge remain siloed across functions/tech. Move toward shared processes and cross-functional planning (store ops, e-commerce, marketing, supply chain, customer service) so decisions are coordinated. (Lecture 3, Slide 45)

### 4) Enable flexible fulfillment using both physical and digital supply chains
Design fulfillment options that use the whole network (stores + DCs) to meet demand: click-and-collect, reserve-online-pickup-in-store, ship-from-store, returns anywhere. This requires integration of physical and digital supply chains for order fulfillment and inventory management across touchpoints. (Lecture 3, Slide 45)

### 5) Build a “single view of the customer” to coordinate service
Use shared customer data so service is consistent across touchpoints (e.g., purchase history, preferences, service tickets). This supports coordinated decision-making and avoids treating the same person as “online customer” vs. “store customer.” (Lecture 3, Slide 45)

<<<STUDENT_QUESTION>>>
How do fulfillment centers play a role in the effectiveness of online retail distribution systems?
<<<END_STUDENT_QUESTION>>>

Fulfillment centers are a core “engine” behind how well an online retail distribution system performs, because they translate online demand into fast, reliable physical deliveries by shaping the distribution structure, warehouse processes, and performance outcomes. (Lecture 11, Slide 46; Lecture 14, Slide 25)

### 1) They determine the distribution structure and customer promise
In e-commerce, the location/number of fulfillment centers (FCs) largely defines how close inventory sits to customers and therefore what delivery speed and coverage you can credibly offer (e.g., next-day vs. 3–5 days). This is part of the broader design choice of distribution structures for conventional retail vs. e-commerce retailers. (Lecture 11, Slide 46; Lecture 14, Slide 25)

### 2) They enable high-throughput warehouse processes that online channels require
Online retail involves many small, fragmented orders and high picking intensity. FC effectiveness depends on warehousing design and processes—especially storage, order picking, and materials handling—because these drive both speed and cost per order. Warehouse layouts and process design are therefore central to online distribution performance. (Lecture 11, Slide 46; Lecture 14, Slide 25)

### 3) They support “value-adding” logistics to speed flow and reduce handling
FCs often rely on value-adding activities like cross-docking (moving goods quickly through the facility with minimal storage) and merge-in-transit (combining items from different sources into one customer delivery). These approaches can shorten lead times and improve delivery reliability—key to online retail effectiveness. (Lecture 11, Slide 46; Lecture 14, Slide 25)

### 4) They depend on Warehouse Management Systems (WMS) to coordinate execution
A WMS helps coordinate inventory visibility, picking tasks, slotting, and shipping operations. In online retail, this coordination is critical to meet tight service targets while keeping errors and labor costs under control. (Lecture 11, Slide 46; Lecture 14, Slide 25)

### 5) They strongly influence supply chain performance metrics (cost, cash, service)
FC decisions affect working capital and logistics performance measures such as inventory turnover and the cash-to-cash cycle. More inventory in more FCs can improve responsiveness, but it often increases total inventory and ties up cash—so FC design is a classic service–cost–capital trade-off in online distribution systems. (Lecture 11, Slide 46; Lecture 14, Slide 25)

### 6) They are a key interface with reverse logistics in e-commerce
Because online retail has significant returns, FCs (or dedicated return facilities) often become nodes for receiving, sorting, refurbishing/restocking, or routing returns—connecting forward distribution to reverse logistics system design. (Lecture 8, Slide 2; Lecture 11, Slide 45)

A manufacturing supply chain creates value through the provision of standardised, repeatable processes that ensure the delivery of freight to the end-customer in a timely fashion.
